news.title: Newsom ‘Not Alarmed’ by DSA Surge—Where 2028 Democrats Stand on Movement
news.text: California Governor Gavin Newsom, long viewed as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, said he is “not alarmed” by the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in a new interview published by Politico, as prospective candidates stake out opposing positions on the organization. Democratic socialists have expanded their power in the primaries during this year's midterms, including Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York, Melat Kiros in Colorado and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania. The DSA has garnered new attention in the wake of the victories, and Democrats are divided about how the party should approach them. Some Democrats view them as a political liability—polls show socialism and democratic socialism are unpopular with voters, and more moderate members of the party fear embracing DSA could alienate moderate and independent voters. But others have said the party should embrace a “big tent” approach ahead of the midterms and 2028, when Democrats will have to walk a fine line to retain support from progressive and socialist voters, while also winning support from moderates, to defeat President Donald Trump and Republicans. What Have 2028 Democrats Said About Democratic Socialism? The first votes of the Democratic primaries will not be cast for more than a year for the 2028 presidential election, but attention has already turned to potential candidates. Some are embracing democratic socialism ahead of potential runs, but others have cast themselves as squarely against the ideology. Here is a look at where the top potential candidates stand on democratic socialism and the DSA. Newsweek reached out to their political teams for comment via email. Gavin Newsom Newsom told Politico in an interview published on Monday that he's “for a big-tent party” when asked about whether Democrats should distance themselves from democratic socialism. “It’s where a lot of the energy in the party is. So why would you ever dismiss that?” the governor asked. Newsom also told reporters in July that whether he joins the race would be determined by “fate.” “I really believe it’s fate,” he said. “You meet the moment; you represent something where you can uniquely and distinctively make the case that your voice matters in a competitive field where there will be stadiums full of Democrats. Every conceivable stripe of Democrat will be on display.” Kamala Harris Former Vice President Kamala Harris has made clear over the years she is not aligned with democratic socialism. “The people of New Hampshire will tell me what’s required to compete in New Hampshire, but I will tell you I am not a democratic socialist,” she said while campaigning back in 2019, when she first ran for president, reported The New York Times. Harris suggested she could run again earlier this year. “I might. I am thinking about it,” she told the Reverend Al Sharpton in April after he asked during the National Action Network’s annual convention if she planned to run for president in 2028. Harris noted that she “served for four years being a heartbeat away from the presidency of the United States.” “I spent countless hours in my West Wing office footsteps away from the Oval Office," she said. "I spent countless hours in the Oval Office and the Situation Room. I know what the job is, and I know what it requires.” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York is the most prominent democratic socialist who has been named as a potential 2028 presidential candidate. She has been a member of the organization and has supported its candidates. As speculation mounts about a potential 2028 run, she recently renewed her membership of the national DSA organization. She discussed democratic socialism in an August 9 interview on ABC News’ This Week, saying there are “fundamental differences” between socialism and communism. “The prevailing one is democracy. And I believe that Democratic socialists are fundamentally pro-democracy. And we believe in the ballot box. We believe in respecting the outcomes of elections and governing democratically and ensuring that the ideas that—and policies that are implemented are won through popular vote and popular opinion,” she said. Ocasio-Cortez addressed presidential speculation in May in a conversation with David Axelrod, who served as an adviser to former President Barack Obama. "My ambition is to change this country,” she said. “Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever. A living wage is forever, workers' rights are forever, women's rights, all of that, and so anyways...to a finer point to your question is that when you aren't attached, when you haven't been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were 7 years old, it is tremendously liberating." In 2016 and 2020, independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders ran in the Democratic primary as a democratic socialist. Jon Ossoff Senator Jon Ossoff, who is up for reelection in swing state Georgia this year, has not made public comments about where he stands on the rise of democratic socialism. He has never publicly identified as a democratic socialist. Ossoff has downplayed speculation that he plans to run, telling MS NOW earlier in the summer, “I have zero interest in running for president in 2028, and frankly zero interest in the 2028 fantasy football right now.” Pete Buttigieg Pete Buttigieg, who served as transportation secretary during the Biden administration, was asked in July about the rise of democratic socialism during an interview on Fox News’ America Reports but largely avoided discussing DSA directly. “There’s always going to be some people in my party who go too far for me, people I disagree with. If you pick the five or 10 or 15 furthest-left people in our party, they're going to, by definition, disagree with a lot of others. But there’s so much that we do, in fact, agree on,” he said. He said in August he is “more inclined than not” to run for president during an appearance on The Diary of a CEO podcast. He said fatherhood has changed how he is approaching whether or not to run. "That's changed all of my equations," Buttigieg said. "It's just something that you really sit with and take seriously, which you should." Andy Beshear Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear said on CBS News' Face the Nation he believes socialism is a “failed experiment” but that “we need to get results for the American people.” He also warned that many Americans are “seeing a system that doesn't work for them.” Beshear has not ruled out a potential run for president. He said during an event hosted by the National Urban League in Nashville, Tennessee, in July that after his last election, he said he would never have to run for anything again. “Sitting here today, I don’t know that's true,” he said. Josh Shapiro Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro has staked out a more moderate lane in the party and has been cheered by that wing as a potential centrist candidate. He told CNN in June that congressional candidate Darializa Avila-Chevalier, who unseated an incumbent in a Democratic primary for a New York City-based House seat, is “not someone who seemingly I would agree with on many things or that we share similar values.” Still, he told MS NOW the following month that the rise of democratic socialism reflects “real passion” in the electorate as well as a “lot of pain” inflicted by Trump. He said during the National Action Network’s annual convention he wants to “be a part of that conversation” regarding 2028. What Is Democratic Socialism? DSA describes democratic socialism as a system "where ordinary people have a real voice in our workplaces, neighborhoods, and society." "We want a democracy that creates space for us all to flourish not just survive and answers the fundamental questions of our lives with the input of all. We want to collectively own the key economic drivers that dominate our lives, such as energy production and transportation. We want the multiracial working class united in solidarity instead of divided by fear," the DSA website reads. DSA members typically support progressive policies like single-payer healthcare and the Green New Deal. The key difference between democratic socialism and other forms of socialism is that democratic socialism maintains that any move toward a more socialist economy must happen through democratic institutions, civil liberties and competitive elections, not through centralized or authoritarian control. The philosophy supports a socially owned economy but believes it should be achieved through political democracy. It also emphasizes individual rights. Merriam-Webster defines democratic socialism as a “political movement calling for the establishment of a decentralized socialist economic system within a democratically run political system.” It defines socialism as “any of various egalitarian economic and political theories or movements advocating collective or governmental ownership and administration of the means of production and distribution of goods.” It’s also different from communism, which is defined as a “totalitarian system of government in which a single authoritarian party controls state-owned means of production.” How Popular Is Democratic Socialism? Democratic socialism continues to be viewed negatively by a majority of Americans even as candidates surged in the 2026 Democratic primaries, according to recent polls. A Marquette Law School poll found that only 21 percent of Americans view DSA favorably, while 48 percent view it unfavorably; 31 percent said they had not heard enough to say either way. Among Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents, 38 percent said they viewed DSA positively, while 21 percent viewed it negatively, according to that poll. Among independents, only 16 percent viewed the group positively, and 46 percent viewed it unfavorably, the poll found. It surveyed 1,001 adults nationwide from May 20-26 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. A Pew Research Center survey from January found that 37 percent of Americans dislike leaders who identify as Democratic socialists, while 17 percent like leaders who identify as one. For comparison, in 2022, 45 percent said they disliked leaders who were Democratic socialists, while 18 percent said they liked them. Among Democrats, 32 percent said they liked Democratic socialist political leaders, while 11 percent disliked them. Among Republicans, unfavorable views stood at 69 percent. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Anna Commander and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: Democratic socialism could become a major sticking point among 2028 Democratic presidential candidates.

news.title: Chris Pappas vs. Karishma Manzur—Final Polls, Odds in New Hampshire Primary
news.text: Progressives are hoping a last-minute surge in momentum can boost Karishma Manzur in the Democratic primary for the New Hampshire Senate race, but Representative Chris Pappas holds a lead in polling and prediction markets. New Hampshire is a Democratic-leaning swing state that backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by only about 3 points in the 2024 election, the most closely divided New England state. But both parties view the race as competitive this year as incumbent Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen is retiring at the end of her term. Democrats believe the national environment, driven by anti-Trump fervor, should keep the seat in their hands, but Republicans believe the candidacy of former Senator John Sununu could make the race more competitive than expected, and a few recent polls suggest a statistical tie. Tuesday's primary will shape the contours of the general election. Pappas has been viewed as the frontrunner, but progressives are hoping Manzur could pull an upset after a recent poll from the University of New Hampshire suggested a tightening race. Sununu is viewed as the favorite in the Republican primary against former Massachusetts Senator Scott Brown. Newsweek reached out to the Pappas and Manzur campaigns for comment via email. Chris Pappas vs. Karishma Manzur: What Polls Show The latest independent poll of the race from the University of New Hampshire showed Pappas up 13 points over Manzur, 47 percent to 34 percent. It surveyed 2,143 New Hampshire residents, including 881 Democratic primary voters, from August 20-24. The poll’s overall margin of error was plus or minus 2.1 percentage points. That marks a narrowing race from UNH’s earlier polls. Pappas led by 24 points in June, 43 points in April and 54 points in January, according to the pollster. Other recent polls have given Pappas a larger lead. A Saint Anselm College poll showed Pappas up 31 points, 59 percent to 28 percent. It surveyed 733 likely Democratic voters from August 17-18 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points among Democratic voters. A GQR poll, a Pappas internal, showed him up 56 points, 71 percent to 15 percent. It surveyed 422 Democratic voters from August 19 to 25, and its margin of error was not published. It was first reported by Semafor. Pappas, who has represented the eastern half of the state in Congress since 2019, is viewed as more moderate. Before entering Congress, he served on the New Hampshire Executive Council. His family owns the Manchester restaurant Puritan Backroom that has been credited with inventing chicken tenders. Manzur has aligned herself with the insurgent progressive movement that has upset the Democratic establishment across the primaries this year. Manzur has emphasized her support for Medicare for All and criticism of Israel as two key differences against Pappas. Pappas Favored in Prediction Markets Pappas also held an advantage over Manzur in the latest data from prediction markets Monday afternoon. On both Kalshi and Polymarket, the Democratic congressman had a 98 percent chance of defeating his progressive rival in the primary. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. Republicans Eye Granite State Republicans see an increasingly competitive race in New Hampshire after two recent polls showed Sununu, the frontrunner in the GOP primary, in a statistical tie against Pappas in the general election. The latest poll from GOP pollster Fabrizio, Lee & Associates showed Sununu receiving 37 percent support and Pappas 36 percent. Other candidates received less than 4 percent support, while 23 percent were undecided about who they would vote for. The pollster surveyed 600 likely voters in New Hampshire from August 27-30, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The UNH poll showed a close race as well. In that poll, Sununu led Pappas by 2 points, 45 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 1,878 likely voters August 20 to 24 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.3 percentage points. However, other polls have been more favorable to Pappas. A Saint Anselm College poll, conducted among 1,411 likely voters August 17-18, showed Pappas up 7 points on Sununu, 48 percent to 41 percent, and 12 points over Brown, 49 percent to 37 percent. A Peak Insights poll, a GOP internal poll, showed Pappas up a point, 43 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 500 respondents June 24-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. No public polls have tested a general election with Manzur as the Democratic nominee, so it’s less clear how she may fare against Sununu. Pappas Sounds Alarm Pappas has sent out several fundraising emails raising alarm about the race, including one titled simply, “We’re losing” sent out last Friday. Some Democrats have been increasingly concerned about the state and have pushed for outside spending to ensure Republicans cannot pull a surprise victory in November, reported The New York Times. Kathy Sullivan, former chair of the New Hampshire Democratic Party, told the newspaper, “I get these ads, emails, pitching donations. They always put up these other states and never New Hampshire. It drives me crazy.” She added: "You’ve got to protect all the states that are close. I just don’t see that happening here the way it should be happening.” Sununu served in the Senate from 2003 to 2009 before losing to Shaheen. He comes from a well-known political family in New Hampshire, as his father and brother are both former governors. The high name ID and popularity of his family in the state adds a layer of uncertainty to the race as Democrats have hoped it would be an easy hold in New Hampshire. Sununu has also consolidated Republican support and has received the endorsement of President Donald Trump. Still, it’s been a tough state for Republican Senate candidates. Shaheen won reelection by more than 15 points in 2020. The state’s other Senator Maggie Hassan, another Democrat, won reelection by 9 points in 2022 after winning her first Senate race by only 1,000 votes in 2016. New Hampshire Leans Blue, But Is Closely Divided The Granite State is roughly evenly divided between Democrats and Republicans. At the federal level, its voters have preferred to back Democrats in recent elections. But it has consistently elected Republican governors at the same time. In the Trump era, Democrats have run strong in Senate races, winning each since 2016. It’s viewed as a politically moderate state with a libertarian streak. Independents are key to the state. As of August 3, 351,815 New Hampshirites were not registered with either party, according to the secretary of state’s office. There were 299,976 registered Republicans and 247,069 registered Democrats. Winning independent voters will be key for either candidate in November. In 2024, the state narrowly went to Harris, 50.7 percent to 47.9 percent. But it gave former President Joe Biden a wider victory in 2020, backing him by 7 points. In 2016, it was one of the country's closest races, backing former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton by less than half a percentage point. However, in 2024, Republican Kelly Ayotte, a former senator, won the gubernatorial race by about nine points. Former Governor Chris Sununu, the brother of John Sununu, easily won in prior cycles. Hassan was the last Democrat to win a New Hampshire governor race in 2014. Can Democrats Flip the Senate? Republicans flipping the New Hampshire Senate seat would complicate Democrats’ narrow path to flipping the upper chamber of Congress. The Democrats already face a difficult Senate map with limited clear opportunities to flip a seat. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate, so Democrats have to pick up four seats in November to win a majority, as Vice President JD Vance is the tiebreaker for Republicans. In addition to New Hampshire, Democrats are defending two seats in swing states won by Trump in 2024—Georgia and Michigan. They view GOP-held seats in Maine, which Trump lost by 7 points, and North Carolina, which he carried by 3 points, as top pick-up opportunities. But there are no other seats up for grabs in states where Trump either won by single digits or lost in 2024, so Democrats have to win in more conservative places like Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas to stand a chance of flipping the Senate. If they win all of the more competitive races, they would have to flip two of those seats. If New Hampshire flips to the GOP, they would have to win three to win a majority, a difficult but not impossible task. What Happens Next Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato's Crystal Ball classify the race as Lean Democratic, meaning it's competitive, but that Democrats do have a slight advantage. Voting hours vary across the state for Tuesday's primary. Polls at many of the largest cities close at 7 p.m. ET, but exact hours depend on municipalities. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Anna Commander and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: A recent poll showed a tightening race between Pappas, a moderate, and Manzur, a progressive, in the Granite State.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: GOP spends Labor Day touting August jobs, Dems lift up union workers
news.text:
It's Labor Day, but as the midterms near, politicians take no days off, and their holiday messaging is falling along partisan lines. 

The White House and Republicans took the day to celebrate a recent win with the stronger-than-expected August jobs report, crediting President Donald Trump as a champion for American workers. 

Democrats took the day to message support for unions and organized labor, a group that has long supported the more-left party. Notably, in 2024, the union group International Brotherhood of Teamsters broke ranks with their decades of tradition endorsing Democrats and chose to not endorse Kamala Harris nor to back Trump. 

The White House touts Trump 

After a stronger-than-expected August jobs report on Friday, Sept. 4, just before Labor Day weekend, Republican messaging on the holiday fell in line with celebration. 

The White House kicked off the weekend on Saturday, Sept. 5, posting, "This Labor Day, we celebrate that more Americans are working than EVER before," and then on Labor Day saying "President Trump will never stop fighting for MADE IN AMERICA."

The Republican Party – which is also spending the day promoting its first-ever midterm convention this week in Dallas – posted a graphic saying that, “MORE AMERICANS ARE WORKING THAN EVER BEFORE THANKS TO PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP” accompanied by the slang term “Jobsmaxxing." The "–maxxing" suffix has been used online to explain doing something to the maximum. 

More: First-ever GOP midterm convention is this week. Here's how to watch

The August jobs report estimated that 162,000 nonfarm jobs were added to the U.S. labor market, after U.S. employers added a now-revised 21,000 jobs in July. The unemployment rate remained at 4.1%, and labor force participation moved up 0.2 percentage points to 61.6%. The White House said after the report that so far during Trump's second term, 1 million private-sector jobs have been created. 

More: August jobs report delivers unexpectedly strong news for US economy

Republican Party Chairman Joe Gruters called Trump the "Jobs President" as he reposted a White House post, writing himself that, "More than 1 million jobs created during President Trumps second term!"

Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, said that the "American worker is WINNING again," adding that "thanks to Republicans, hardworking Americans have more opportunities and can keep more of their own hard-earned money." Johnson said Americans are experiencing bigger paychecks, no taxes on tips or overtime and a boom in U.S. manufacturing.

The president himself did not post about the successful job numbers on Labor Day – though he did the day before – instead using the holiday to post a partisan attack, saying on Truth Social: " Happy Labor Day to all, including the Radical Left Lunatics, Communists, and Dumocrats who will do anything possible to destroy our Country. These Deranged People, after fighting for 10 years, should finally acknowledge that your Favorite President (ME!), knows how to WIN! They should be exhausted by now but, sadly, they’re not." 

The president, who is speaking at the Republican midterm convention this week, continued: "They’re going to give it one last shot at ruining America, but we’re not going to let that happen. We’re going to win the Midterms, BIG, and SAVE AMERICA!" 

Democrats message to union voters 

While Republicans tout the labor report, Democrats are appealing to union workers – a voter base that is core to the party. Democrats have not completely lost that base, but there has been a trend of blue-collar workers moving away from the party, according to a survey by Center for Labor and a Just Economy in collaboration with the Columbia Labor Lab. 

The Democratic Party took to social media Monday morning with post including a graphic that reads "Unions Built the Middle Class," writing that, "Thanks to our labor unions, America’s workers have stronger benefits, fairer wages, and safer working conditions."

The messaging that celebrated unions was similar from Democratic leaders across the country, including from both the established faction and more left-leaning progressives, who have been at odds this midterm primary season. Here's what some of them had to say: 

Former President Joe Biden: "I’ve said it my entire career: the middle class built America. And unions built the middle class. To every worker who's ever punched a clock, worked a double, or walked a line for fair wages – and to everyone who stands up for them, at the bargaining table, in the statehouse, or on the shop floor: thank you. This country runs in large part because of you."New York Sen. Chuck Schumer, Democratic minority leader: "Happy Labor Day! Workers and unions are the backbone of our economy, and we owe them our gratitude today and every day."Former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, who has signaled a likely 2028 presidential run: "The 40-hour work week. The weekend itself. Lifesaving safety standards. Organized labor has changed our country for the better. This Labor Day, we recognize the achievements of our unions and the workers who make the American way of life possible."California Gov. Gavin Newsom: "Labor Day is a reminder of a simple truth: WORKERS built this country. But today, too many Americans are working harder, paying more and falling further behind — while Donald Trump gets richer and hands more wealth to the people at the very top. Working people built America. This November, it’s time to take our country back."Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego: "We need to be for a pro-labor, pro-worker agenda. That starts with: Increasing the federal minimum wage from a poverty wage to $20/hr. Doubling the pay for overtime. Requiring overtime pay on federal holidays. Protecting workers' right to bargain for better pay, benefits, and safer workplaces."Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan: "The labor movement gave us weekends, 8 hour work days, and ensured that our kids can go to school rather than work. Honored to fight for unions every day. Happy Labor Day to all those who have fought for a fairer economy in the richest country in the world."

Democratic socialist leader and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders is an independent – not a member of the Democratic Party – but shared a similar celebration of union workers, posting: "On this Labor Day we give our thanks to the millions of trade unionists in our country who are leading the fight for economic, social and racial justice. Thanks to all of you for what you’re doing. Let’s go forward together."

Contributing: Rachel Barber

news.title: Obama mocks 'poo smelling' Trump for 'only changing his own nappy' as health fears grow
news.text: Barack Obama brutally mocked 'poo smelling' Manbaby Donald Trump for never changing a nappy – apart from his own. A resurfaced clip shows Obama discuss buying diapers after his eldest daughter Malia was born. As he discusses the cost of living, he jokes: "I remember the first time I went into the store. I was like... 'What?' Do you see how much diapers cost? I remember buying diapers. Do you think Donald Trump has ever changed a diaper?" Crowds chuckled during the the speech – which he gave during the 2024 Presidential campaign – when one wag shouted out "his own". Obama, himself laughing, said: "I almost said that, but decided not to." The clip is being widely shared on social media two years on from the rally in Pittsburgh, where he was campaigning for Democrat candidate Kamala Harris. One Twitter user said: "Setting up a joke, letting a fan finish the punchline, and then claiming you 'decided not to say it' while giggling at the microphone is top-tier political comedy. Bro has mastered the art of the un-said insult." Another said: "Obama knew exactly where that joke was going and still kept it classy. That “I almost said that” was the perfect punchline. Some people lead with insults; Obama leads with wit." A third replied to the clip, posting: "Thank you for reminding me what it’s like to smile a real, warm, and genuine smile when listening to a President speak." The resurfacing of the clip comes after wild claims emerged Trump "poos himself so much you can smell him around the corner" amid fears his health is in severe decline. But not everybody seemed to agree the Orange Manbaby changed his own nappy. One Twitter user suggested that was actually a job for his 'Nappy Nurse' Natalie Harp, the fiercely loyal aide who never seems to leave his side. They wrote: "Sorry, Mr. President [Obama]. That’s Natalie’s job." Harp earned her crude nickname after it was claimed the large black tote bag she regularly carries is filled with adult nappies for Trump. She is also dubbed the "human printer" for constantly trailing Trump to hand him hard copies of flattering news stories and cherry-picked data. And she was recently seen by eagle-eyes wags online clutching a mysterious black rectangular gadget, sparking wild rumours that it was a device keeping the President awake and alert during meetings.
news.summary: A resurfaced clip shows Barack Obama poking fun at Donald Trump, saying he probably never changed a nappy before suggesting he may wear one – and social media users are going wild for it

news.title: Kamala Harris Responds to Attack on Ohio Democrat Amy Acton: 'Political Violence Has No Place in Our Nation'
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris responded to the news that Ohio Democrat gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton was reportedly attacked while attending a fair, stating that “political violence has no place in our nation.”

In a post on X, Harris expressed that she was “horrified by yesterday’s attack” against Acton, and added that she was “grateful” for actions of law enforcement officials and other people who “stayed to help attend to the injured.”

“I am horrified by yesterday’s attack on Amy Acton in Ohio and grateful for the the actions of law enforcement and others who helped — including Dr. Acton herself, who stayed to help attend to the injured,” Harris wrote. “Political violence has no place in our nation. People must be safe to participate in our government and electoral process without fear of violence.”

Harris’s post comes after Acton’s campaign issued a statement on Sunday that explained that “while attending the Canfield Fair, an armed individual lunged at Dr. Acton, injuring multiple people.”

“Dr. Acton and Eric are grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured,” the statement continued. “This kind of violence has no place in Ohio.”

Breitbart News’s Matt Mercer reported on Sunday that “a report from WOIO-TV said the individual responsible for the attack was booked into the Mahoning County Jail on two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct”:

A report from WOIO-TV said the individual responsible for the attack was booked into the Mahoning County Jail on two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct.
A witness said a “suspect who had weapons was arrested the Mahoning County Democratic Party tent after knocking volunteers to the ground.”
Local media did not indicate the severity of those injured.

Republican Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign issued a statement in response to the news of the attack on Acton, stating that the incident that occurred is “completely unacceptable and has no place in politics.”

“Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence,” Connie Luck, who serves as the Communications Director for Vivek for Ohio said in a statement. “What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope that no one was hurt.”
news.summary:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris responded to the news that Ohio Democrat gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton was reportedly attacked while attending a fair, stating that "political violence has no place in our nation."

"While attending the Canfield Fair, an armed individual lunged at Dr. Acton, injuring multiple people. Dr. Acton and Eric are grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured. This kind of violence has no place in Ohio. Dr. Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another," said Addie Bullock, communications director for the Acton campaign.

— Dr. Amy Acton (@amyactonoh) September 6, 2026

There's just one problem. This story is a complete lie.

That statement is carefully worded to make you think Acton was standing in a gunman's crosshairs. She wasn't. Acton was never touched, never injured, and never threatened.

An armed man pushed through a crowd at the Canfield Fair on Sunday, knocking down two elderly fairgoers before deputies tackled him and placed him under arrest. Within hours, her campaign and a sympathetic press corps turned an arrest for disorderly conduct into an assassination attempt.

The campaign lied.

Yet, the New York Times, of all outlets, couldn't even back up the Acton campaign's version of events.

"An armed man was arrested Sunday after forcing his way through a crowd toward Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for Ohio governor, the authorities said," the paper reported. "Dr. Acton was giving a speech at the Mahoning County Democratic Party tent at a fair in Canfield, in the northeastern part of the state, when a man pushed through the crowd, knocking over two elderly audience members, according to the county sheriff, Jerry Greene, and two witnesses. The man did not draw his weapons, according to Sheriff Greene and the witnesses. Dr. Acton was not injured."

Had there been even a hint of evidence that this was an assassination attempt or some form of attack against a political candidate, you can bet law enforcement would have treated it as such. But, law enforcement officials made it quite clear there was no assassination attempt, and the suspect is facing misdemeanor assault charges.

The Mahoning County Sheriff's Office identified the man as Patrick Havas, an Ohio resident, and released his mugshot after the incident inside a crowded tent at the Canfield Fair near Youngstown. Havas faces two counts of assault for knocking over those elderly attendees and one count of disorderly conduct. He carried two firearms in holsters under a valid Ohio concealed-carry permit and never drew either one. Officers only discovered the guns after they already had him in handcuffs.

ICYMI: Democrats Have a Midterm Secret They Don’t Want Voters to See

Despite the fact Acton was never in any harm, Democrats piled on like Acton was the victim of political violence.

"I just spoke to Amy Acton. She's tough. There's no place in our society for political violence. An issue that unfortunately Gabby and I are very familiar with. I want to thank law enforcement for stopping this attack. Perpetrators of political violence must be brought to justice," Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) wrote on X.

He wasn’t alone. Pete Buttigieg also chimed in. “There is no place for political violence in our country. I'm grateful that Amy is safe and thankful for the law enforcement officers who acted swiftly today. Attacks like this cannot just be the price you pay for running for office. This must never become normal," he wrote.

Kamala Harris, never one to miss a press opportunity, also posted a statement. "I am horrified by yesterday's attack on Amy Acton in Ohio and grateful for the the actions of law enforcement and others who helped — including Dr. Acton herself, who stayed to help attend to the injured. Political violence has no place in our nation. People must be safe to participate in our government and electoral process without fear of violence. The hate and division that dominate our political discourse must end," she said.

Even Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) joined in. "I'm thankful Amy Acton is safe. My thoughts are with everyone who was injured, and my gratitude goes out to law enforcement for responding quickly and getting the situation under control. Political violence should be concerning to all of us, it has no place in our democracy," he wrote.

None of them waited for the sheriff's report. None of them checked the facts first. They ran with a fake version of events because the story fit a narrative they'd already decided to sell.

So, why did the Acton campaign play the victim here? That’s easy to figure out. 

Acton is locked in a dead-heat race against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. The most recent poll has Ramaswamy up three points, though Acton clings to a 0.3-point edge in the RealClearPolitics average. A race that tight needs a catalyst to generate a wave of anger, enthusiasm, donations, and a base fired up enough to show up on Election Day.

On top of that, Democrats have tried desperately since the assassination attempts on Donald Trump and the assassination of Charlie Kirk to convince the country that political violence is a "both sides" problem.

Make no mistake about it, the Acton campaign made a desperate move here and the New York Times, of all outlets, just handed everyone the receipts proving the campaign lied.

news.title: Stephen A Smith blasts podcast hosts for rude off-camera behavior after he recorded three-hour show with them
news.text:
Stephen A. Smith has gone scorched earth at podcast hosts Cari Champion and Jemele Hill after giving them three hours of his time for a recent episode.

Smith was a high-profile guest for the Flagrant and Funny podcast last week, appearing with his two former ESPN colleagues for a wide-ranging discussion.

But it was the hosts' off-air behavior that left Smith disappointed, after he revealed they didn't thank him, and that he overheard disparaging remarks from the pair after they had finished recording. 

'I sat down for three hours,' Smith revealed on his own, self-titled podcast. 'Three hours with these two ladies, Jemele Hill and Cari Champion. I didn't know what they were going to ask, other than about the NABJ (National Association of Black Journalists), and of course the Jasmine Crocketts and Kamala Harris' of the world.

'There was no prep, there was nothing orchestrated. I rolled up in there and one of the first things I did after saying hello, was making sure it was very, very clear to them, I've got nothing but time. And yet I see them, post-show, talking about interpretations, what people are insinuating, comments emanating from people about them.

'I even heard Cari Champion say, "I don't know if it benefited us". Really? Ladies and gentlemen, when I showed up at that show the other night, they had 9,000 subscribers and their largest video was at about 35,000, of any show they had done.

'Once I sat down with them, they've picked up over 30,000 subscribers, they've had over 1 million views - 500,000 over YouTube - but Cari Champion is saying she doesn't know if it did them any good. A simple thank you would have sufficed.'

Champion has since posted a video to her Instagram page - recorded on her beach vacation - in which she offered her thanks to Smith for appearing on the show.

Hill, meanwhile, has not yet referenced the First Take host's criticism of their behavior.

Smith also took umbrage with the podcast's decision to edit some of his comments, claiming that he now wants a video copy of every interview he does going forward.

'I'm not doing any more interviews on YouTube without folks agreeing to make sure that it is completely unedited and that the comment section remains open and that I get a video copy of the interviews that I do,' he said. 'I don't think that's unreasonable to ask for.

'I don't think that I should sit down for 3 hours feeling I was promised - my team was promised - an unedited version that would be put out there to the masses, and that I'm deprived of that. 

'I don't appreciate that. I want that interview, Cari, Jemele, and to your team. I want that interview in its entirety put up for everybody to see, showing what was cut out.'

The interview with ESPN star Smith, which was published in two separate parts on YouTube, now has close to a million views on the platform, with the next nearest clip only racking up 40,000.
news.summary: Smith was a high-profile guest for the Flagrant and Funny podcast last week, appearing with his two former ESPN colleagues for a wide-ranging - and lengthy - discussion over a glass of wine.

news.title: Cropped Out Of The Frame: Gloria Steinem’s Final Missed Opportunity [Op-Ed]
news.text:
CIA asset. Former Playboy bunny. The face of the feminist movement. 

Those are three ways headlines have described feminist Gloria Steinem since her passing at the age of 92. To read just those three things about a major figure like Steinem, it’s easy to draw conclusions about who she was. 

For Steinem, those three descriptors are more misleading than they are helpful. They completely miss the reality of her legacy and ignore the Black women who shaped it. 

When you consider that Steinem was a white feminist credited with leading the women’s movement, the lens narrows even further. Most of the coverage of Steinem so far has maligned, if not completely erased, the Black women who inspired her and who were instrumental in building and growing the women’s movement. 

Steinem’s stint as a Playboy bunny was short-lived and never meant to be considered a core part of her career trajectory. She went undercover as a reporter at the Playboy Club for a story for Show magazine and exposed the underbelly of Hugh Hefner’s business hidden behind all its marketed glitz and glamour. Through her reporting, she discovered Playboy bunnies were forced to work long, grueling hours, experienced constant sexual harassment, and in most cases were compensated far less than advertised. 

Part of her reporting also unearthed that Black women hired to become Playboy bunnies were marginalized and often referred to as “Chocolate Bunnies.” This firsthand look at how Black women bore the brunt of sexism and racism in the industry added to her early understanding of how overlapping oppressions showed up in the lives of Black women. 

Just as mainstream media hyper-focused on her stint as a Playboy bunny, they also latched onto her early intelligence ties. Steinem has claimed over the years that her associations with the CIA have been overblown and misconstrued. She has stated that the organizations she worked with to coordinate attendance at international youth festivals received funding from the CIA but that she was never asked to report on American nationals or assess foreign nationals. However, within the Black community where the CIA’s historical weaponization against civil rights leaders during that era remains a deep wound, this chapter of her life continued to spark intense skepticism and, in many ways, complicated her relationship with the Black community. 

To call Steinem the face of the feminist movement is perhaps the most accurate descriptor, but it is also where the erasure of Black women is perhaps the most glaring. She became the face of the feminist movement even as she frequently credited Black women for teaching her through their example, showing her how to resist and fight for equality. 

Dorothy Pitman Hughes was one of those Black women who, if racism had not trumped sexism in feminist circles and in the larger media landscape, would have easily emerged as the face of the movement either above or right alongside Steinem. 

Steinem first met her in the late 1960s while working as a reporter assigned to interview Hughes about her pioneering work at a childcare center in New York. The two became close friends and would go on to travel across the country together, speaking out on behalf of women’s rights. In 1971, they took the infamous black-and-white photograph showing both of them with their fists raised in solidarity. 

Although Steinem regularly credited Hughes with coaching her on how to become a polished public speaker, deepening her understanding of racism, and schooling her on issues like childcare, Steinem was pushed to the forefront as the most visible representative of the women’s movement. When the two traveled together, Steinem got most of the media’s attention, while Hughes was pushed to the margins and largely ignored. 

Over the years, while Steinem continued to solidify her status as the most well-known feminist in the country, she kept positioning herself alongside powerhouse Black women. This was true even as mainstream media continued to crop them out of the prevailing narratives about the fight for women’s equality. 

When Steinem founded Ms. Magazine in the 1970s, she entrusted trailblazing authors and editors like Alice Walker and Margaret Sloan-Hunter to help shape the publication’s editorial voice. 

Even with those efforts, systemic erasure persisted, and Walker ultimately resigned from the magazine in 1986 after becoming frustrated with the ongoing lack of diversity on its covers. In her resignation letter, she addressed the dearth of Black women on the cover, writing, “In real life, people of color occur with much more frequency,” and then added, “I do not feel welcome in the world you are projecting.” 

When Shirley Chisholm ran for President in 1972, Steinem championed her groundbreaking campaign. Steinem’s commitment to shifting political power and putting the American presidency in the hands of a woman for the first time continued into recent years, when she supported both Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris’ runs for President. 

Steinem’s activism continued until the very end. Ever the masterful strategist, Steinem left us with one final essay, a final interview, and what is expected to be her final book as the ultimate contributions to her own legacy. 

Her final lengthy TV interview, taped a couple of years before her death, was part obit and part personal farewell to everyone watching. It debuted on Netflix the day she died as Famous Last Words: Gloria Steinem, and featured a sit-down interview between her and series creator Brad Falchuk. 

When discussing her role as the most visible leader of the feminist movement, Steinem pinned it down to pure endurance. She noted that her other partners in the struggle for women’s rights had children and other careers, leaving her to simply outlast them. At no point did she mention the racism her peers experienced from the media and beyond that maligned them and kept them from achieving higher visibility. 

For a Black audience looking at how she is remembered and who among us has been forgotten and maligned, this final goodbye exposes a hard truth. By taking the reins to control her final narrative across multiple platforms, Steinem had a prime opportunity to forcefully push Black women into the center of the frame. She could have spent her parting words focused on Black women and other maligned communities who built the foundation right beside her and those who are doing the important work of pushing for equality now. Sadly, she chose not to.

What’s expected to be her last book, An Unexpected Life, will be released later this month. Her last essay appeared in The New Yorker the day she died, and perhaps the most resonant part of that essay was her reminder that the greatest challenge to equality is those who benefit from inequality. And that those people are often people whose “power rests on the group they were born into” and who “fear what might happen if they have no built-in advantage.” Touché, Ms. Steinem, touché.

That commentary on built-in advantages makes her final onscreen action even more ironic and disappointing. At the very end of her Netflix documentary, she looked directly into the camera to deliver a final message to the audience, explicitly asking viewers that the most important thing we can do for each other is to share our own stories and “know each other through stories.”

While asking the audience to claim their own narratives sounds powerful, it still allows Steinem’s towering, white legacy to obscure the Black women who made her activism possible. This was her final opportunity to truly give back to Black women by platforming and centering us. She could have compelled the public to face our erasure, and she could have pushed the next generation of white feminists to become better allies than she ultimately proved to be. 

Instead, her silence became the final anchor for her whiteness. Black women built the foundation for her stage, only for us to be left sitting alone in the dark when her curtain finally closed.

news.summary: OPINION: Mainstream media loved Gloria Steinem’s image, but her final goodbyes left the Black women in the shadows.

news.title: Jon Ossoff pulls level with AOC on 2028 presidential prediction market as race heats up
news.text:
Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff has surged level with New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in the race to find the Democratic Party’s next presidential nominee, according to Coinbase’s live prediction odds.

Ossoff and Ocasio-Cortez were tied on a 17 percent likelihood of becoming their party’s choice for the White House as of Monday morning, leaving the long-term front-runner, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, in third place on 14 percent. 

Ossoff, who was elected to his seat in January 2021, just one day before the Capitol riot erupted in Washington, D.C., recently made headlines by mocking President Donald Trump at a rally in Atlanta. 

“He doesn’t want to do his job,” the senator said of the president in comments that quickly went viral. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

The reference to Trump’s executive assistant Natalie Harp drew a furious response from both the president – who angrily likened Ossoff to the 1980s children’s entertainer Pee-Wee Herman – and the White House, which inadvertently prolonged the controversy by aggressively going on the attack.

Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s recently departed press secretary, Communications Director Steven Cheung and spokesman Davis Ingle all viciously rebuked Ossoff, as did CNN’s resident conservative Scott Jennings, demanding that he apologize for the insinuating remark. 

Cheung called him “Jon Jackoff” and “the biggest cuck loser in politics” while Ingle referred to him as “a cringeworthy, feminine theatre kid cosplaying as Barack Obama” but the senator was unmoved, preferring to stand back and marvel at the “meltdown” he had inspired. 

Ocasio-Cortez, a well-known Capitol Hill progressive, recently attracted attention by announcing she had frozen her eggs, which some interpreted as a signal that she was putting her maternal ambitions on hold in order to pursue a tilt at the White House. 

Her recent move to walk back some of the “woke” rhetoric she and others engaged in in 2020 met with a similar reaction and was received by some as a conscious effort to reposition herself closer to the center. 

As for Newsom, who has also enjoyed trolling Trump on social media over the last year, he admitted his trip to South Carolina last week was made with at least one eye on a presidential run. 

Neither Ossoff nor Ocasio-Cortez nor Newsom has formally announced their intention to launch a presidential campaign, answering cagily when asked and treating the idea as premature, given that the midterms have not even taken place yet.

Meanwhile, most conventional political surveys – as opposed to betting markets – still put former vice president Kamala Harris in pole position, as she has prior experience of mounting a national campaign, albeit at short notice and unsuccessfully.

Harris said last month she had “not made a decision” on a potential 2028 run.

“I am fully, sincerely, focused on these midterms,” she told her audience at the National Urban League conference in Nashville, Tennessee, alluding to her campaigning efforts on behalf of such candidates as James Talarico in Texas.

However, she did outline some fresh policy positions, including expanding the Supreme Court and making statehood available to Puerto Rico and D.C., suggesting she has at least given some thought to her next career move.
news.summary: Georgia senator who made fun of President Donald Trump’s relationship with his aid Natalie Harp, drawing an angry reaction from the White House, is being tipped as his potential successor in the Oval Office

news.title: Filmmaker Alex Gibney Says New Elon Musk Documentary 'Upends The Myth' Of Tech Titan's Genius
news.text: VENICE, Italy — Documentary filmmaker Alex Gibney says his nearly four-hour film "Musk," which premiered this week at the Venice Film Festival, dismantles the popular image of Elon Musk as a modern-day inventor, arguing instead that the billionaire's true skill lies in convincing investors to believe in visions that rarely align with reality.Gibney, whose past subjects have included Enron, Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, the Church of Scientology, and U.S. military abuses at Bagram and Abu Ghraib, told The Associated Press that nothing in his career compares to the sheer scope of power held by Musk. Bleecker Street is set to release the documentary in theaters in October.Asked why he chose to make a film about Musk, Gibney said the project began with an outside pitch in early 2023 that he was initially hesitant to pursue."A number of people came to me a few years ago, actually early 2023, and said, would you like to make a film about him?" Gibney said. "And I initially wasn't sure, but a really good friend of mine convinced me that it was a good idea because it would be a portrait of kind of 21st century power. And so with that, I dug in."Gibney said his research led him to a conclusion that reframes the source of Musk's influence entirely, tracing it not to invention but to his ability to project confidence about ambitious futures."I think the source of his power comes from, how should I put this, bulls---?" Gibney said. "That is to say, his ability to speak with confidence about the future in ways that convince people to invest in his companies. It's really a future that rarely is in sync with facts or evidence or any remote possibility. So that is really what I discovered. That and the fact I think his genius, if there is a genius, is that he is not an inventor, he's an investor. His genius is stock pumping."The documentary also examines Musk's political shift toward President Donald Trump, a move Gibney said surprised many who had previously viewed Musk as a favorite of environmentally minded audiences because of his leadership at Tesla. Gibney said his research pointed to two underlying motivations he had initially underestimated."I discovered two things," Gibney said. "One is, in a way, it was a predictable transition because he goes where the federal government money is. But the other reason is his companies were facing an enormous number of federal investigations. And indeed, Tesla was under criminal investigation. But out of that case, there was a good chance that under a Kamala Harris administration, he might go to prison. He joked about that on the Tucker Carlson show. I think those were two key motivators that I had initially underestimated."Gibney said common explanations attributing Musk's political shift to opposition against progressive social movements did not hold up under closer scrutiny."A lot of people clocked it to the woke mind virus," Gibney said. "After doing some research, I didn't see it that way."Reflecting on how Musk compares to the other powerful figures and institutions he has profiled throughout his career, Gibney said the scale of Musk's influence stands apart, even as the underlying psychological pattern feels familiar."Nothing compares to this in terms of the scope of his power," Gibney said. "What's interesting about Musk is it's not so much something that's new as an old wine in a new bottle." Gibney described Musk as exhibiting what he called "noble cause corruption," in which a genuine belief in an important mission, in Musk's case making humanity multiplanetary and advancing sustainable energy, becomes a justification for increasingly questionable conduct in pursuit of that goal."Musk is not dissimilar from the guys at Enron," Gibney said. "He's not dissimilar from Elizabeth Holmes in the way that he bent the truth to serve his impulses. The one big difference with Musk is that he has companies, SpaceX and Tesla, which contain a great number of very qualified engineers and executive leaders."Gibney's film has already drawn a public response from its subject. Musk previously called the documentary a "hit piece" on social media, prompting a direct reply from Gibney asking how Musk could make that judgment. Asked whether he approaches his subjects willing to have his own assumptions challenged, Gibney said bias is inevitable but that he remains committed to following facts wherever they lead."There is always bias, but I'm always willing to have my assumptions challenged," Gibney said. "I started off as a kind of an admirer and was honest in my desire to want to talk to him, but ultimately he didn't want to talk to me. Then you start digging into the facts and you follow them where they lead. And where they led for me was to a place that upended the myth, I would say, of Elon Musk as a kind of modern Leonardo da Vinci."Asked whether Musk attempted to interfere with the film's production, Gibney said the more significant obstacle came not from Musk directly but from the fear he inspired in people close to him, including both supporters and critics within his companies."He didn't really except in so far as the fact that people were terribly afraid to speak to me on the record, or at least on camera," Gibney said. "They were just terrified of Elon. And these were people in his companies. These were people who knew him well. These were supporters and critics. A lot of people close to him who were his admirers would say, 'I can't talk to you unless I get Elon's permission.' I thought, wow, for such a big and powerful person, that seems awfully weak."Given the film's nearly four-hour runtime, Gibney addressed a question he said comes up frequently when people learn of the project's length."When I told people that there was going to be a nearly four-hour Elon Musk documentary, the first question was 'did he make it about himself?'" Gibney was asked, to which he responded that the film differs substantially from other recent documentaries centered on public figures close to political power, joking that "this probably doesn't share that much with the Melania documentary." Gibney added that despite its serious subject matter, he intended the film itself to remain engaging for audiences."One of the things I would say about the film is it's a dark and dangerous topic, but the film itself is a fun ride," Gibney said."Musk" is among the most anticipated titles at this year's Venice Film Festival, arriving amid sustained public fascination with the billionaire's expanding influence across technology, politics and global business. With its theatrical release set for October through Bleecker Street, the documentary is expected to reignite public debate over Musk's legacy and the sources of his power, following its high-profile premiere on the festival's international stage this week.

news.title: AP Decision Notes: What to expect in New Hampshire’s state primary
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Two former Republican U.S. Senators eyeing a return to Washington will compete in New Hampshire’s state primary Tuesday for a seat they’ve both sought previously with mixed results. In the Democratic primary for the same U.S. Senate seat, a four-term congressman faces an increasingly competitive challenge on his left flank from a democratic socialist candidate.

Voters will also select nominees for U.S. House, governor and other state offices.

The race to replace retiring three-term Democratic U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen is one of a handful across the country that could determine control of the U.S. Senate for the second half of President Donald Trump’s final term. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to retake the chamber, and keeping New Hampshire in their column is a key part of that effort.

In the Republican primary, former U.S. Sens. John Sununu and Scott Brown are among eight candidates seeking the nomination. Sununu won the seat when it was last open in 2002, defeating then-Gov. Shaheen, but she ousted him in 2008 after one term. Brown was elected in Massachusetts in 2010 to serve out the remaining three years of the late Democratic U.S. Sen. Edward Kennedy’s final term. After his defeat for a full term in 2012, Brown moved to New Hampshire and challenged Shaheen in 2014, losing narrowly.

Brown endorsed Trump just ahead of his 2016 New Hampshire presidential primary victory. Trump later appointed Brown to serve as U.S. ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa in his first term. Trump is now backing Sununu over Brown in the primary, despite an ongoing war of words he’s had with the Sununu family over the years.

Sununu endorsed Trump’s rival Nikki Haley for president in 2024 and penned an op-ed that year under the headline “Trump is a loser.” That echoed a critique Sununu’s father, former White House Chief of Staff John H. Sununu, made of Trump during the 2016 presidential primaries, when he told ABC News that Trump had been “a loser all his life.” Trump called the elder Sununu “ a main loser.”

The former senator’s brother, former Gov. Chris Sununu, also endorsed Haley in 2024 and once called Trump “ (expletive) crazy.” Chris Sununu was one of the president’s top Republican critics and was a frequent target of Trump’s ire on social media.

Sununu has outraised Brown for the campaign overall, $4.1 million to about $2.2 million, although Brown has spent more of his haul than Sununu. Sununu had about $3 million remaining in his campaign account as of Aug. 19, compared to about $417,000 for Brown.

Americans for Prosperity Action, a super PAC tied to the conservative Koch political network, has spent at least $3.3 million on the race since June 30 in support of Sununu and against U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, the Democratic front-runner.

The Republican field includes state Rep. Brian Cole, auto dealership owner Anthony DiLorenzo and iron works CEO Hollie Noveletsky.

When do polls close?

Poll closing times vary across the state. Most polls close at 7 p.m. ET, but some close at 7:30 p.m. or 8 p.m. ET.

What’s on the ballot?

The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners in contested primaries for U.S. Senate, U.S. House, governor, executive council, state Senate and state House.

Who gets to vote?

Registered party members may vote only in their own party’s primary. In other words, Democrats can’t vote in the Republican primary or vice versa. Independent or undeclared voters with no party affiliation may participate in either primary, but voting in a primary will affiliate them with that party. New voters may register on primary day at a polling site, but the deadline to change party affiliation for voters who are already registered was in June.

How many voters are there?

As of Aug. 3, there were about 899,000 registered voters in New Hampshire, including about 300,000 Republicans, 247,000 Democrats and about 352,000 undeclared voters.

How many people actually vote?

About 148,000 Republican primary ballots and about 96,000 Democratic primary ballots were cast in the 2022 state primaries.

About 135,000 Republican primary ballots and about 118,000 Democratic primary ballots were cast in the 2024 state primaries.

How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?

About 8% of Democratic primary ballots in both the 2022 and 2024 state primaries were absentee ballots cast by mail or in person. In recent Republican state primaries, absentee votes made up 4% of the total vote in 2022 and about 5% in 2024.

The New Hampshire Secretary of State has not disclosed the number of absentee ballots cast ahead of Tuesday’s primary.

When are early and absentee votes released?

New Hampshire runs elections at the town and city level. There are 238 separate jurisdictions administering local elections, and they vary in terms of how and when they release results. Most of the larger jurisdictions in the state release all or nearly all their results from both absentee and in-person Election Day voting in their first vote updates of the night. Other large jurisdictions release a mix of results throughout the night.

In the 2024 state primary, the AP first reported results at 8:03 p.m. ET, or three minutes after the last polls closed. The vote count passed the halfway mark at 9:37 p.m. ET. The last vote update of the night was at 2:04 a.m. ET with about 92% of total votes counted.

When will the AP declare a winner?

The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.

How do recounts work?

There are no automatic recounts in New Hampshire, but in state primaries, a losing candidate may request and pay for a recount if the margin is 10 votes or less than 1.5% of the total vote. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Are we there yet?

As of Tuesday, there will be 56 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

news.title: In Trump’s second term, the MAGA merchandise boom is going bust
news.text:
BOONES MILL, Va.—Donald “Whitey” Taylor made a fortune from sales at Trump Town USA, his store selling Make America Great Again apparel and memorabilia related to President Trump.

Taylor’s Boones Mill store—a former church—brought in upwards of $15,000 a day in 2024, the best sales pace in the business’s 11-year history, he said. But more than a year into Trump’s second term, sales have sunk. Taylor, 76 years old, said he now averages just $1,500 a day, a slump he attributes to customers’ struggles with higher gas prices due to the Iran war and persistent inflation.

“You get used to good money, and you still want to make it,” said Taylor, reflecting on the hundreds of patrons a day who used to bustle through his store aisles. “Today, the economy is just not worth a crap anymore.”

Many customers also stopped buying new merchandise because they felt they had already done their part in getting the president elected to a second term, he said.

Many MAGA-centered merchandise retailers and their suppliers are seeing sales dwindle, according to interviews with wholesalers, sales representatives, business owners and employees. As the president’s approval rating hovers near all-time lows, imperiling Republicans’ control of Congress, store owners blame a stagnant economy and weaker MAGA enthusiasm for lower sales. Some stores are closing permanently.

The Trump Store Manchester shut its doors recently, citing weak sales and high operating expenses due to increased rent and advertising costs, according to an employee. In the store’s final days, steep discounts to clear inventory didn’t draw a flood of customers. Only about 12 customers a day frequented the Manchester, Tenn., store’s final 72 hours, the employee said.

Suppliers have adjusted their inventory to reflect weaker Trump merchandise sales.

Quan Ngo helps operate NT Souvenir Wholesale, a Washington, D.C.-based souvenir supplier that sells ornaments, magnets and political merchandise of both Republican and Democratic politicians to businesses throughout the country.

Ngo said he knew Trump would win in 2024 after sales of merchandise supportive of the president dominated those in support of former Vice President Kamala Harris’s campaign. He said politics doesn’t drive his business; money does. And because of weak sales, he has cut back on purchasing Trump merchandise and lets inventory—much of which is made in China—run low.

“We don’t make decisions off of emotions, we make them off of certainty and whether there is a demand,” he said. “We’ve ordered less Trump merchandise because demand is down.”

Lisa Hall, an independent sales representative based in Syracuse, N.Y., sells nearly two dozen product lines, including Trump-related merchandise. She said sales for Trump apparel began falling after Trump’s re-election but took a nosedive roughly six months ago—just after the U.S.-Iran war kicked off. She said that while many of her clients continue to purchase MAGA apparel, they aren’t buying as much and are reaching out far less frequently than they used to.

“I used to be hearing from them; my phone would be exploding. Now, that’s not happening,” she said.

Hall said sales are weaker because of economic worries. If it boils down to buying a toy for their child or a MAGA hat, customers are going to choose the toy, when they might have purchased both in a better economy, she said.

Not all store owners say they are struggling. Seth Hansen, the owner of the Trump Store Branson in Branson, Mo., said that while sales are lower than the election-year high, business is still good. He also operates a Jesus-themed merchandise store nearby, but the Trump store has continually performed better, raking in seven figures in revenue last year, he said. Hansen said other stores might be having trouble due to weak business sense.

“They’re not businesspeople,” he said of store owners who are struggling. “They love Trump and the Republican Party and what it stands for, but that’s not a business plan.”

In Boones Mill, patrons still treat Taylor, who carries a small pistol in his back pocket, as a celebrity. Passersby and truck drivers honked and waved as he was closing shop for the day, wearing Trump-themed sneakers and socks imprinted with Confederate flags.

Trump won more than 70% of Franklin County, where the town is located, in 2024, among the highest margins for the president in the state. Twila Brisco, 81, who lives in nearby Roanoke, said the store is a vital landmark to preserving Trump’s legacy. At checkout, Taylor and Brisco shared memories from their youth and high school. Brisco said she talks to her grandchildren about preserving conservative values.

Taylor, who is still an ardent Trump supporter, said he is offering more America 250 merchandise as well as Confederate memorabilia, but it hasn’t helped much. He is waiting for Jan. 20, 2029, anticipating that when Trump leaves office for good, nostalgic MAGA supporters will return in droves and help sales reach their former highs.

“They’ll all be back. It’s going to be awesome,” he said.

news.title: For low-income Michiganders, federal changes could land on housing
news.text:
One year into President Donald Trump’s second term, the waves of policy change are reverberating in Wayne County. In Detroit, first-time homeowner Tamika Simley is trying to hold it all together, juggling mortgage payments, groceries, gas, and utilities on a budget that keeps getting tighter.

“You’re having to pick and choose between things, and you shouldn’t have to,” Simley said in an interview earlier this year. “Why should I have to choose between my rent or my mortgage and feeding my family?”

While Simley’s story is personal, it reflects a much broader struggle now facing thousands of Wayne County residents as federal policy shifts take hold.

Though some of the steepest cuts do not fully kick in until 2027, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed by President Trump in 2025, slashes funding and imposes stricter eligibility limits for SNAP and Medicaid. Combined with changes to federal housing programs and increased housing costs, experts say strained budgets could affect housing stability for some Wayne County families.

​​Supporters of the OBBBA say the changes are intended to reduce federal spending, tighten eligibility requirements, and encourage workforce participation in public assistance programs.

But in a county where many rent and the poverty rate far exceeds the state average, local officials warn these federal cuts will force thousands of residents to make impossible choices to remain in stable housing. As Michigan heads into pivotal midterms, state and local governments are scrambling to fill the gaps left by the federal government.

Julie Cassidy, a senior policy analyst at the Michigan League for Public Policy focusing on the social determinants of health, cites the change in housing costs as a main concern − especially rising rent prices, as more than one-third of households rent in Wayne County compared to 27% statewide.

According to federal guidelines, housing is considered affordable if it costs no more than 30 percent of a household’s income. But in Wayne County, many are far beyond that limit.

“We consistently find in every community that renters are having to spend a lot more of their income on rent than homeowners do, and their housing costs are increasing more quickly. In Wayne, the median rent is 38 percent of the median household income,” said Cassidy.

U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Detroit, who recently lost a bid for re-election in a district with one of the nation’s highest poverty rates, said earlier this year his constituents are acutely aware of how federal policy is hitting their pocketbooks.

Life has become more expensive in Trump's tenure, Thanedar said. "He says he’s going to work on lowering costs, and he talked about inflation. He said that he alone can fix all that, because he is such an economic genius. In reality, prices have gone up substantially, and housing costs have gone up."

While recent policy changes have intensified these problems, Thanedar acknowledges that many of Detroit’s challenges have deeper roots. “These are not all problems that happen under the Trump administration," he said, citing longstanding issues with things like public transportation and affordable housing.

Nick Cook, director of public policy at the Michigan Coalition Against Homelessness, warns that the impact of rising rents and reduced assistance will extend beyond immediate housing insecurity.

“It's going to impact their housing security; it's also going to impact their ability to keep jobs, which will then impact their ability to maintain housing. So it's really the second-order effect, we're seeing this maybe a year to two years down the line,” said Cook.

More: Trump administration halts work to prevent carp chaos in Great Lakes

More: Detroit aims to bring 9K rentals to code by September 2027

Cook said Michigan’s Housing Choice Voucher program is already under strain.

“The wait lists have been turned off for a couple of years now just because of the increasing cost of rentals. We’ve seen rent increase by 25 percent since 2020 in Michigan. So there are just not as many vouchers to go around. So it is hard to keep somebody stabilized and keep them in housing on top of the attacks,” Cook said.

Cook pointed out that the state now faces a shortage of 195,000 affordable units for low-income residents. Data from Wayne Metropolitan Community Action Agency’s 2026 Community Needs Assessment show that financial instability is widespread in the county, even among working families. Most surveyed households earn less than $50,000 a year, and nearly all respondents say high utility costs and covering basic needs are major challenges.

For Simley and others, these numbers translate into tough, daily decisions about what to pay for first, with utility payments, she said, an “outrageous” expense. When her daughter was first in college, Simley qualified for subsidized housing for a year, which made all the difference.

“It was great when I had it, because it kind of took some of the sweat off my brow, so to speak. I was able to, you know, afford groceries and things without worrying about, let me penny pinch here, and penny pinch there,” said Simley.

Cassidy said when families face budget constraints, they nearly always prioritize rent or mortgage payments, even if it means cutting back on groceries or skipping medical care. That’s become even more common as safety net programs come under strain.

With the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s new restrictions taking hold, advocates worry that families already stretched thin will be forced to cut back even more on essentials like food in order to keep a roof over their heads. Additional federal changes are still ahead, including stricter eligibility redeterminations and more frequent income checks for programs like SNAP and Medicaid beginning in January 2027—raising concerns that more residents could lose coverage or assistance.

As the debate continues and changes loom, Detroit has often found itself thrust into the national political arena. In October 2024, Trump claimed that if Kamala Harris wins the presidency, “the whole country will end up being like Detroit.”

For Tamika Simley, those words miss the real story. “I think they need to drop him off on Mac and Bewick for about two weeks… Your music came from here. Your cars came from here, there’s a lot of firsts that came from Detroit,” said Simley.
