news.title: Republican midterm convention will be ‘Trumpist pageantry’ - at the party’s own risk
news.text:
It seemed like a good idea at the time. In December 1978, Jimmy Carter, a US president besieged by inflation and energy crises, watched as thousands of Democrats descended on Memphis, Tennessee, for a rare midterm convention.

“It was wild,” recalls Elaine Kamarck, who attended as a 28-year-old working for the Democratic National Committee. “It became a forum for Ted Kennedy to informally announce his opposition to president Carter. There was a lot of hostility to the president there. The Democrats have sworn ever since never to do anything this stupid again.”

The 1978 convention took place after midterm elections in which Democrats suffered losses but still maintained control of the House of Representatives and Senate. The party also held midterm conventions in 1974 and 1982. Kamarck, who later served in the Bill Clinton administration, adds: “The Democratic party has never thought of doing this again and, whenever it has, people like me say, ‘No, are you absolutely crazy?’”

Republicans, however, did not get the memo. This week in Dallas, Texas, the party will stage a midterm convention for the first time. Donald Trump will deliver a keynote address on Wednesday and closing remarks on Thursday in Dallas, Texas. Other speakers include Vice-President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr and the president’s son Donald Trump Jr. The convention has been billed as a “primetime showcase” to boost morale, nationalise congressional elections and galvanise Republican voters.

But success is far from guaranteed. The made-for-TV spectacle clashes directly with the two opening games of the American football season. A Politico website survey of more than 70 Republican candidates and members found 45 who either do not plan to go to Dallas or are still thinking about it. Some cited prior commitments while others balked at the $25,000 price of attending.

Unlike conventions in a presidential election year, delegates will not be making party rules or drawing up a policy platform. “This is essentially a Trump rally that they’re calling a midterm convention,” said Kamarck, now a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington. “They’re trying to get enthusiasm among their base because that’s what they need for November. Basically, this is a Trump show.”

That ambition probably made sense when the midterm convention was first mooted. Republican voters are historically slow to turn out when Trump is not on the ballot. By putting himself on the marquee, the president – who defied the odds to win the White House in 2024 – is hoping to narrow the enthusiasm gap.

Among those hoping for a boost from Trump in Texas is Senate candidate Ken Paxton, whose history of scandals – including an affair and securities-fraud indictment – could prove costly against the Democratic rising star James Talarico.

But now it appears the plan could backfire. Trump’s approval rating is ‌at 33%, the lowest point of his political career, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll last week. Democrats seem more fired up about the midterms with 46% describing themselves as “very enthusiastic” ​about voting in November, compared with 31% of Republicans.

Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill, warns that building a midterm convention around a failing president is tantamount to “political suicide”.

“It is an incredibly risky strategy for any Republican at this point to hitch his wagon to Donald Trump,” she explained. “On every issue that Trump was once strong on he is underwater, from the economy to immigration.”

Setmayer, co-founder of the political action committee the Seneca Project, added: “The idea that he’s going to excite people is flawed at this point, given the polling numbers in Donald Trump’s own constituency. They’re not inspired and this vanity convention is not going to change that with 60 days to go to the election. If anything, it’s going to remind people of how dissatisfied they are under Donald Trump’s second term.”

There are further signs that the president could be more of a curse than a blessing. Some candidates are quietly scrubbing his likeness from their websites in a tactical retreat. In Texas, candidate Carlos De La Cruz replaced “TRUMP CONSERVATIVE” with “PROVEN CONSERVATIVE” on his homepage, erasing a line about being “ready to be President Trump’s wingman in Congress” for a platitude about “servant leaders”.

In Kentucky, Ralph Alvarado pivoted to “INDEPENDENT LEADERSHIP”. In Nevada, Martin O’Donnell, a music composer best known for his work on the Halo video game series, no longer features his Trump endorsement photo on his website. In south Texas, Eric Flores replaced “SUPPORT PRESIDENT TRUMP’S AGENDA” with “LOWER THE COST OF LIVING”. In Alaska, Nick Begich edited his homepage to a simple: “We have delivered for Alaska.”

Elsewhere, candidates are actively breaking ranks. The Wisconsin congressman and gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany publicly rebuked Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario as “Lake America” and opposed importing cheaper ground beef. The Michigan congressman Tom Barrett is campaigning on his votes to limit Trump’s war in Iran, highlighting his support for the War Powers Resolution.

Trump, however, appears unmoved and indifferent. Allan Lichtman, a history professor at American University in Washington, said: “He doesn’t care about any of these other candidates. He only cares about two things when it comes to the midterms: one, that he won’t be investigated and two, that he can get his appointments through the Senate. He demands loyalty for everyone else and gives loyalty to no one.”

A Republican source said at least 100 members of Congress were expected to attend the convention and more than 20,000 tickets had been distributed, ensuring a packed arena.

The source denied that Trump would dominate proceedings, insisting that the convention would aim to “energise our base, inform folks there is an election and highlight the contrast between what Republicans are offering – which is a secure border, safe communities, cutting taxes, giving Americans more freedom – and what the Democrats are offering, which is reopening the borders, repealing the tax cuts, investigating, obstructing, impeaching President Trump and not having an agenda beyond that”.

The source also rejected reports that Republican candidates were distancing themselves from the president, saying: “We have Republican candidates across the country who want the president in their districts. You see it with Mike Lawler, who’s one of two Republicans left in Congress still in a district that Kamala Harris won in 2024. I believe the president has campaigned for him in his district twice. Mike Lawler does a very good job of embracing the president’s policies. He deviates on certain issues when needed.”

The convention schedule will also aim to steady the ship. The first night will include segments focused on tax cuts, healthcare affordability, the border, trade and domestic manufacturing, with appearances by “workers and everyday Americans”.

The second will highlight families benefiting from policies like no taxes on tips, overtime and social security, as well as overseas prisoners who have been released, border security, efforts to lower prescription drug costs and a tribute to the slain rightwing activist Charlie Kirk.

The convention will also try to appeal to the “Maha” – or Make America healthy again – wing of the party, with a segment targeting corporate influence in the treatment of chronic diseases. And it will mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks with families of first responders.

But the program makes no mention of any programming related to foreign policy or the deeply unpopular war in Iran.

Lichtman observed: “People aren’t buying what they have to say, which is things are getting better, it’s the golden age, prices are coming down, we’re winning the Iranian war, our immigration policy is great. They’re not gonna buy it just because it’s a convention. Plus, as we know, Trump always goes off script and that’s never helpful to his party.”

But Republicans do seem to believe they have an ace up their sleeves. Trump and his allies are expected to go in hard on a theme pointing to the primary election successes of democratic socialists and casting Democrats as godless communists and Marxists who pose an existential threat to the American way of life.

Charlie Sykes, a conservative broadcaster and author of How the Right Lost Its Mind, said: “The midterms will either be a referendum on Donald Trump, in which case they will be disastrous for the Republicans, or Republicans will hope that they can make this a referendum on the radicalism of Democrats, so I’m guessing that will be a major theme.

“The big question is, who is going to be paying any attention to this? Who is going to be watching this other than the hardcore base, the already convinced? I have a very hard time imagining independent voters tuning in to see the Trumpist pageantry.”

But commentators believe that the convention, with its potential to draw primetime TV viewers and generate viral clips, could make a difference in the margins. Larry Sabato, director of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, said: “It might increase Maga’s turnout. That’s the only positive in this thing potentially for Republicans.

“It’s not going to change any minds but it might convince the Maga people, ‘Well, I don’t normally vote when our hero is not on the ballot but if this is what Donald wants me to do, I’m going to pitch in and help.’ But it’s not going to help that much.”

The midterm convention could have an intriguing subplot. Along with Vance, the Texas senator Ted Cruz and other potential 2028 presidential contenders will be in attendance for what could be an early audition. Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center thinktank in Washington, said: “Anybody who looks in the mirror and sees a president looking back at him or her, if those people are speakers, it will be a chance for them to make an impression.”

Such aspirants would be wise to tread carefully, however, since Trump is not likely to cede the limelight willingly. Sykes added: “It is a Trump-a-palooza and once again Donald Trump insists on being – what was the old phrase about Teddy Roosevelt? – the bride at every wedding and the corpse at every funeral.

“He wants to make the midterms all about himself despite the fact that he’s reaching the Nixon line in terms of polling unpopularity. It’s very much on brand except that right now, with every day we get closer to the midterms, Trump’s narcissism becomes a greater challenge to Republicans who want to survive what looks like a blue wave.”

news.title: The DSA’s late Senate challenge highlights an uncomfortable truth for New Hampshire Democrats
news.text:
With just three primaries left on the calendar, this long season is finally nearing its finale. Most of Democratic energy is focused on primaries past, notably Michigan, Texas and Maine. This makes some sense. All of those states are very important seats that the party needs to either hold on to or flip in November. But there’s one state that Democrats still need to defend that has gone largely unnoticed: New Hampshire.

After Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced her retirement last year, New Hampshire’s Senate seat has been assumed to be leaning blue, with Rep. Chris Pappas expected to safely sweep the nomination on Sept. 8. But as a fellow teacher tells Arnold Schwarzenegger in the philosophical classic, “Kindergarten Cop,” “Kindergarten is like the ocean. You don’t want to turn your back on it.”

Pappas and establishment Democrats should probably have treated this election like kindergarten — or at least, like the ocean.

Instead, for much of his campaign, Pappas seemed to turn his back on Democratic Socialists of America challenger Dr. Karishma Manzur. As recently as two months ago, a local news station didn’t even mention the name of the candidate challenging Pappas for the nomination, focusing most of the interview on his likely general election opponent, former New Hampshire congressman and Sen. John E. Sununu. Sununu held the seat from 2003 to 2009 before losing to the retiring Shaheen. As a result, he remains a well-respected and familiar face in Granite State politics.

Since that interview, however, Manzur has proven herself to be a worthy primary opponent, and the DSA has emerged as a national force to be reckoned with. And with days to go, democratic socialists in the state are trying to make the race in New Hampshire interesting, too. This is a problem not because Pappas could lose — still an unlikely scenario — but because the last-minute flurry is diverting attention from a general election contest that could end up being pivotal for Democrats’ Senate hopes. And it’s highlighting Pappas’ weaknesses even as he prepares to move on to the next round.

Last week, the University of New Hampshire released a poll showing Manzur has considerably closed the gap. The poll had Pappas leading Manzur 47% to 34%, with 18% still undecided. Also concerning, Pappas was polling under 50% for the first time, which is never a good sign entering the last couple of weeks of an election.

While it remains improbable that Manzur will actually win, we should remember that this has been an unpredictable campaign cycle. In Florida’s Senate primary last month, state lawmaker and democratic socialist Angie Nixon stunned the establishment by defeating the much more nationally known Alex Vindman, who gained widespread recognition for his role in President Donald Trump’s first impeachment trial. Plus, with such a large number of voters still undecided, stranger things have happened.

Pappas has been campaigning for well over a year. He has racked up the expected endorsements, including a recent one from former Vice President Kamala Harris, and everything points to him winning his primary. However, he has, until recently, largely been running what I’d describe as a relatively paint-by-numbers effort.

And this could ultimately lead to an even bigger problem for Pappas and the Democrats after this primary because there is an excellent chance that New Hampshire becomes a true toss-up race in November. In the same University of New Hampshire poll, Pappas is now polling behind Sununu 43% to 45%, while 5% said they would vote for another candidate if the race were held today and 7% remained undecided. (In other words, the race remains a statistical tie.)

So while trying to pick up four Republican seats, Democrats may also have to go all in to avoid losing New Hampshire. That’s a scenario the Democrats definitely do not want to turn their backs on.

news.title: Higher rates spell an end to the case for putting huge programs on Uncle Sam’s credit card
news.text:
As the United States emerged from the COVID-19 pandemic, interest rates were ultra-low, making borrowing ultra-cheap and sort of removing one concern as lawmakers pushed for massive fiscal stimulus packages.

Many on the Left — such as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) — advocated the Green New Deal, which would have leveraged federal spending to curb climate change and create a federal jobs guarantee, to the tune of trillions of dollars.

That, and programs such as Medicare for All, were big talking points for Democrats running in the 2020 presidential election. Some, such as Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ), cosponsored Green New Deal legislation, and others, like former Vice President Kamala Harris, explicitly called for such a plan.

Likewise, 2020 contenders, including Sanders, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), and former New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio, all fully endorsed Medicare for All, while several other candidates, including Booker and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), also supported it.

But since then, the political calculus for Congress spending trillions of dollars on these massively ambitious policy proposals has lost steam. In part, because borrowing costs would cause any such plans, without pay-fors, to spike the national debt even further after it just crossed $40 trillion.

The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury security, for instance, has risen from around 1.5% at the end of 2021 to 4.75%.

Ryan Young, a senior economist at the Competitive Enterprise Institute, said that a lot of those proposals, once considered politically viable for Democrats, would have a difficult time getting enough votes — even if Democrats had the trifecta of the White House, Senate, and House of Representatives.

“The spendiest of the spendy policies, like the Green New Deal, a Medicare for All proposal, a lot of things that maybe DSA types are proposing, they fall flat with the rest of the party,” Young told the Washington Examiner. “And frankly, that super spendy wing of the party has been mostly confined to college campuses.”

Young said that spending plans such as these now have a fundamentally different fiscal calculation than they did in the early 2020s, when they were major talking points.

“And I don’t think your average voter is going to be attuned to this, but interest rates are a big reason why,” he said. “I was looking at the 10-year bond rates, which are creeping up to 5%. A few years ago, they were as low as 1%.”

Higher yields make borrowing and financing such massive spending proposals much, much more expensive. And some Democrats even blanched at the price tags back when rates were very low. For instance, then-Sens. Joe Manchin (D-WV) and Kyrsten Sinema (D-AZ) used their leverage to reduce the size of Biden’s Build Back Better agenda.

But now that rates are higher, it makes spending ever more perilous.

In February, the Congressional Budget Office projected that federal debt held by the public would reach 101% of GDP this year. By 2030, debt will exceed 108% of GDP, surpassing the all-time high during World War II. The CBO said debt is projected to be 175% of GDP by 2056.

A big concern with higher yields on Treasuries will be the increased cost that the government will incur in servicing that debt.

Federal government payments on interest have risen to nearly 4% of GDP, up from 2.5% at the end of 2021. Interest costs have not been this high since the 1990s, when pressure on the federal government’s finances led to a deal to balance the budget between then-President Bill Clinton and the GOP.

Former Rep. Carolyn Bourdeaux, a Georgia Democrat who is now the executive director of the Concord Coalition, which focuses on balancing the budget, told the Washington Examiner that for every tenth of a percentage point that gets added to the yield, some $380 billion in net interest over 10 years is added.

“So it has an enormous impact,” she said.

Ditch said that with the fiscal concerns, higher yields, and mounting debt, there “isn’t sort of the almost the consensus position” among Democrats to push for these big-ticket spending items.

Some of the most ambitious spending programs were lauded by evangelists of modern monetary theory, which essentially posits that concerns about spending shouldn’t necessarily constrain governments.

“I guess it’s using the monetary printing press as a first resort rather than a last resort,” Young said of MMT as a philosophy.

Young said that such economic policies lead to inflation, which is now the No. 1 issue that voters are concerned about.

“The MMTers have been pretty quiet since COVID because they did all the spending programs that they wanted, and then we got inflation because of it,” he added.

And even before this year, many Democrats backed off endorsing sweeping spending legislation like the Green New Deal after inflation shot through the roof under Biden’s first term following the pandemic stimulus spending.

For instance, in 2024, when Harris was running for president, the Washington Examiner first reported that she had reversed her support for a federal jobs guarantee, a key pillar of the Green New Deal.

A federal jobs guarantee would mean that the federal government would provide a job to anyone who wants one, a massively costly proposal that harkens back to the New Deal policies of the 1930s.

Also, while some, like Ocasio-Cortez, who are aligned with the more socialist wing of the party, will likely still push for big spending programs like Medicare for All, others seen as frontrunners for 2028, like Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-CA), are unlikely to do so.

“If we look at some of the more prominent names who are people being talked about in terms of 2028, Gavin Newsom isn’t someone who’s going to be promoting an MMT-style Medicare for All kind of agenda,” Ditch said, adding that he also didn’t get the sense that Harris was pushing for that in 2024.

news.title: Elon Musk is no genius inventor — he’s a ‘stock pumper,’ filmmaker claims
news.text:
Documentary filmmaker Alex Gibney has spent his career investigating powerful institutions and controversial figures, from Enron and Elizabeth Holmes to Scientology and abuses at Bagram and Abu Ghraib. But he says none compares with the power wielded by his latest subject: Elon Musk.

Gibney's nearly four-hour documentary, "Musk," premieres at the Venice Film Festival this week ahead of an October theatrical release from Bleecker Street. The filmmaker said the project attempts to dismantle the mythology surrounding the billionaire and examine the origins of his extraordinary influence.

The project began in early 2023, when producers approached Gibney about making a film on Musk. He was initially reluctant until a friend convinced him the billionaire offered an ideal lens for examining "21st-century power."

Once he began investigating, Gibney said he came to believe Musk's greatest talent was not invention but his ability to sell investors a vision of the future.

"His genius, if there is a genius, is that he is not an inventor, he's an investor," Gibney said. "His genius is stock pumping."

Gibney also examined Musk's political shift toward President Donald Trump, which surprised some former admirers who had viewed the Tesla chief as a champion of clean energy.

The filmmaker said he concluded that Musk's political evolution was driven partly by his companies' reliance on the federal government and partly by the regulatory and legal scrutiny they faced.

"He goes where the federal government money is," Gibney said.

He also pointed to federal investigations involving Musk's businesses, including a criminal investigation into Tesla, as a possible factor in Musk's political calculations. Gibney argued those pressures were more significant than the cultural explanations often offered for Musk's shift to the right.

Musk has previously joked that he could face prison under a Kamala Harris administration. Gibney said he initially underestimated how important the prospect of continued federal scrutiny was to Musk.

Comparing Musk with previous subjects, Gibney said he saw similarities with disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and figures involved in the collapse of Enron, particularly in what he characterized as their willingness to bend facts to pursue larger ambitions.

However, Gibney acknowledged a significant difference: Tesla and SpaceX are functioning companies staffed by large numbers of accomplished engineers and executives.

He described Musk as an example of "noble cause corruption," in which someone becomes so convinced of the importance of their mission that they begin to justify questionable behavior as necessary to achieve it.

"Nothing compares to this in terms of the scope of his power," Gibney said.

Musk has dismissed the documentary as a "hit piece," but Gibney rejected suggestions that he began the project determined to attack him.

The filmmaker said he initially approached the project as an admirer of Musk and wanted to interview him, but Musk declined to participate.

"You start digging into the facts and you follow them where they lead," Gibney said. "And where they led for me was to a place that upended the myth, I would say, of Elon Musk as a kind of modern Leonardo da Vinci."

Gibney said one of the biggest challenges was persuading people who knew or worked with Musk to speak publicly.

He said employees, supporters and critics were reluctant to appear on camera because they feared the billionaire's reaction. Some admirers told Gibney they would not speak without Musk's permission.

"They were just terrified of Elon," Gibney said. "I thought, wow, for such a big and powerful person, that seems awfully weak."

Despite the documentary's serious subject matter and lengthy running time, Gibney said he wanted the film to remain entertaining.

"It's a dark and dangerous topic," he said, "but the film itself is a fun ride."
news.summary: Alex Gibney's new documentary “Musk” premieres this week at the Venice Film Festival

news.title: Documentarian Alex Gibney on the power and influence of Elon Musk
news.text:
Alex Gibney has made films about powerful people, corporations and organizations before: Enron, Elizabeth Holmes, Scientology and the U.S. military’s abuses at Bagram and Abu Ghraib are just a few. And yet, he said, nothing compares to the scope of power held by his latest subject, Elon Musk.

With a nearly four-hour runtime, “Musk” is having its world premiere this week at the Venice Film Festival. It's one of the most hotly anticipated of the festival and the year — Bleecker Street is releasing it in theaters in October. 

Gibney spoke to The Associated Press about upending the Musk myth, his revelations about his power and his support of President Donald Trump. 

Remarks have been edited for clarity and brevity.

 AP: Let’s start with the obvious, simple question: Why Elon Musk? 

GIBNEY: A number of people came to me a few years ago, actually early 2023, and said, would you like to make a film about him? And I initially wasn’t sure, but a really good friend of mine convinced me that it was a good idea because it would be a portrait of kind of 21st century power. And so with that, I dug in.

 AP: The nature and scope of his power is something that remains a little mysterious. Can you go into a little bit about what you found and how your film addresses that? 

GIBNEY: In some ways it’s a simple story (with) a lot of complicated details. I think the source of his power comes from, how should I put this, (expletive)? That is to say, his ability to speak with confidence about the future in ways that convince people to invest in his companies. It’s really a future that rarely is in sync with facts or evidence or any remote possibility. So that is really what I discovered. That and the fact I think his genius, if there is a genius, is that he is not an inventor, he’s an investor. His genius is stock pumping. 

The other thing I discovered was that the reasons for turning toward Trump were both a break with the past, I mean, people look to the way that he was idolized by many people on the, you could call it the left, or people who regarded him as a kind of climate savior for what he was doing with Tesla. Many people wondered about that transition. I discovered two things. One is, in a way, it was a predictable transition because he goes where the federal government money is.

But the other reason is his companies were facing an enormous number of federal investigations. And indeed, Tesla was under criminal investigation. But out of that case, there was a good chance that under a (Kamala) Harris administration, he might go to prison. He joked about that on the Tucker Carlson show. I think those were two key motivators that I had initially underestimated. A lot of people clocked it to the woke mind virus. After doing some research, I didn’t see it that way.

 AP: You’ve covered powerful people and companies before in your films. Does anything compare to this? 

GIBNEY: Nothing compares to this in terms of the scope of his power. What’s interesting about Musk is it’s not so much something that’s new as an old wine in a new bottle. And Musk, I think like some of the characters that I’ve followed in the past, is afflicted with what some people call noble cause corruption. That is to say, you begin to believe in a cause. And in Musk’s case, it was making us multiplanetary and also leading us into a more sustainable environmental world. And because you’re in line with those important, valuable, good causes, anything you do in the service of those causes is OK. And ultimately that leads you to corruption.

In a way, Musk is not dissimilar from the guys at Enron. He’s not dissimilar from Elizabeth Holmes in the way that he bent the truth to serve his impulses. 

The one big difference with Musk is that he has companies (SpaceX and Tesla) which contain a great number of very qualified engineers and executive leaders. 

 AP: There was the famous social media exchange where Musk called the film a hit piece and you responded, “How would you know?” Do you go into your films willing to have your assumptions challenged? Was bias involved? 

GIBNEY: What is it that physicist Richard Feynman used to say? It’s good to have an open mind, but not so open that your brains fall out. There is always bias, but I’m always willing to have my assumptions challenged. I started off as a kind of an admirer and was honest in my desire to want to talk to him, but ultimately he didn’t want to talk to me. Then you start digging into the facts and you follow them where they lead. And where they led for me was to a place that upended the myth, I would say, of Elon Musk as a kind of modern Leonardo da Vinci.

 AP: Did he try to interfere? 

GIBNEY: He didn’t really except in so far as the fact that people were terribly afraid to speak to me on the record, or at least on camera. They were just terrified of Elon. And these were people in his companies. These were people who knew him well. These were supporters and critics.

A lot of people close to him who were his admirers would say, “I can’t talk to you unless I get Elon’s permission.” I thought, wow, for such a big and powerful person, that seems awfully weak. 

 AP: When I told people that there was going to be a nearly four-hour Elon Musk documentary, the first question was “did he make it about himself?” 

GIBNEY: This probably doesn’t share that much with the Melania documentary.

One of the things I would say about the film is it’s a dark and dangerous topic, but the film itself is a fun ride.

news.title: America’s War on Iran Has Always Been a Bipartisan Effort

American bombs are now falling on Tehran, and while Donald Trump ultimately pulled the trigger, administrations before him—Republican and Democrat alike—constructed the gun, and even loaded it.

In 1995, US president Bill Clinton issued executive orders banning US investment tied to Iran’s petroleum sector and, soon after, most US trade with and investment in Iran. His administration justified the sanctions with an accusation that would later be used against Saddam Hussein’s Iraq not even a decade later: “Iran’s efforts to acquire weapons of mass destruction” and their alleged support for terrorism.

The International Atomic Energy Agency, which had visited Iran a few years prior to inspect their nuclear activity, reported no evidence of nuclear weapons.

In 1996, Congress followed up with the Iran and Libya Sanctions Act, which passed 415-0 in the House, and by unanimous consent in the Senate,targeting foreign and US companies investing more than $20 million a year in Iran’s energy sector.

Much like embargoes on Iraq, which were linked to catastrophic civilian deaths, over time, American sanctions on Iran decimated the economy and its people by devaluing currency, shrinking living standards, and limiting access to food and medicine.

In 2000, a report by a neoconservative think-tank called Project for the New American Century warned that even if Saddam Hussein were removed, “the need for a substantial American force presence” in the region would remain because “Iran may well prove as large a threat to US interests in the Gulf” as Iraq has.

Several prominent figures involved with the think-tank later joined the Bush administration, including Donald Rumsfeld, Paul Wolfowitz, and John Bolton.

In 2001, shortly after 9/11, Iran offered counter-terrorism assistance to the US, but instead, President Bush lumped them in with Iraq and North Korea under an umbrella he termed the “Axis of Evil”. Clinton-era sanctions were kept in place, new ones were added, and covert measures began to undermine the Iranian establishment.

That same year, Congress passed the Authorization for Use of Military Force by a vote of 420-1 in the House and 98-0 in the Senate, granting the president sweeping authority to use military action against those connected to the 9/11 attacks. Although Iran had no connection to 9/11, the deliberately broad language of the bill created a permanent legal framework for military action across the Middle East without requiring new congressional approval.

Towards the end of Bush’s final term in office, a 2007 US National Intelligence Estimate (a comprehensive report involving all US intelligence agencies) concluded with “high confidence” that Iran was not currently building a nuclear weapon.

Still, Barack Obama’s policies continued beating the drums of war.

In 2010, he significantly expanded financial sanctions on Iran’s oil, gas, and banking sectors, measures that severely restricted access to essential medicines in Iran, which passed the House 408–8 and the Senate 99–0.

At the same time, his administration intensified Bush-era cyber operations against Iranian nuclear facilities. The Stuxnet computer worm, reportedly developed by the US and Israel, was credited with disabling hundreds of centrifuges and delaying enrichment efforts, even though the nuclear program continued to show no signs of weaponization.

In 2015, Obama concluded a nuclear deal that imposed strict limits on Iran’s nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief. But its premise was a masterclass in propaganda that worked to build further consensus for war, first by painting Iran as an aggressor, and second by continuing to perpetuate a narrative that it was interested in pursuing nuclear weapons, despite continued evidence to the contrary.

Meanwhile, far more aggressive American allies in the region—namely Israel—were exempt from such scrutiny, with their own nuclear stockpile shrouded in secrecy and tucked away from international oversight of any kind.

After the nuclear deal lifted certain sanctions in 2016, Iran’s economy rebounded. And yet at the same time, US and Israeli hawks continued to fret, alternating their fearmongering and moving the goalpost away from Iran’s nonexistent nuclear weapons and instead towards their regional influence and ballistic missile program.

Republicans and Democrats joined together the following year to pass new sanctions on Iran’s missile program, along with entities tied to the Revolutionary Guard. These measures were approved with a vote of 419-3 in the House, 98-2 in the Senate.

Fortunately for the many warmongers adorning both major political parties, the arrangement with Iran had been signed late into Obama’s second term, paving the way for a new president to conveniently overturn it.

In 2018, Donald Trump did exactly that. His administration unilaterally withdrew from the deal and reimposed sanctions. In April 2019, the US designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Iran’s most powerful military and political force, as a foreign terrorist organization. The following year, Trump ordered a drone strike that killed Qassem Soleimani, head of the Guard Corps’ Quds Force, a dramatic escalation.

Taking office in January 2021, the administration of Joe Biden largely maintained Trump’s “maximum pressure” framework, leaving existing sanctions in place, along with Trump’s designation of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard.

And while Biden campaigned on rejoining the nuclear deal, once in office, he demanded Iranian compliance as a prelude to sanction relief, which effectively made it impossible given growing Iranian distrust for the US.

In late 2022, after being asked about the nuclear deal by a woman appearing to wear a hair ribbon in Iran’s flag colors, Biden reportedly responded that the deal was “dead”, adding, “I know they don’t represent you, but they will have a nuclear weapon.”

Two years later, an assessment from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence found that Iran “has undertaken activities that better position it to produce one, if it so chooses” but added that “the Intelligence Community continues to assess that Iran is not building a nuclear weapon.”

Even so, in October 2024, when asked who she thought America’s “greatest adversary” was, Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris replied: “I think there’s an obvious one in mind, which is Iran.”

Harris, like Trump, repeated the lie that Iran was in the business of pursuing nukes, saying the US “will not allow Iran to obtain a nuclear weapon. Period.” And like Trump, she maintained that “all options” remained on the table to keep them from obtaining nuclear weapons, including military force.

In 2025, a majority of Democrats voted with Republicans to hand the Trump administration $900 billion in military spending, which provided funding for Pentagon operations, weapons procurement, overseas deployments, and military readiness programs for the upcoming fiscal year.

At nearly every stage, Republicans and Democrats in Congress, along with presidents from both major parties, have laid the foundation for a war on Iran.

The Bush administration lied its way into an invasion of Iraq, but nobody was held accountable. The Obama administration expanded the Bush-era Authorization for Use of Military Force to include drone-bombings in at least seven different countries, along with the targeting of US citizens accused of terrorism, and again, nobody was held accountable. Trump built on these precedents during his first term not only by amping up Obama’s drone strikes, but also by assassinating an Iranian commander. Again, no accountability. The Biden administration funded Israel’s flattening of the Gaza Strip while also shielding it from repercussions at the United Nations and International Criminal Court, effectively demonstrating that the so-called rules of international law were never fair, but instead, selectively applied.

Over time, escalation itself became normalized.

Economic warfare became cyber sabotage. Cyber sabotage became targeted assassinations. What were once extraordinary war powers became permanent executive authorities. By the time Trump entered the White House for his second term, the framework for America’s long-awaited war on Iran was already in place.

All he had to do was pull the trigger.

news.title: Susan Sarandon’s Political Views: Where She Stands and Which Actors Support or Oppose Trump
news.text:
Susan Sarandon has spent decades using her celebrity to advocate for progressive causes, oppose U.S. military intervention and challenge both major political parties. But she does not fit neatly into the Democratic Party establishment — and her sometimes harsh criticism of Democrats has periodically created the impression that she was sympathetic to Donald Trump.

That characterization is misleading.

Sarandon’s political record is better understood as progressive, anti-war, economically left-wing and skeptical of the Democratic establishment. She supported Bernie Sanders in the 2016 Democratic primary, later endorsed Green Party candidate Jill Stein and has repeatedly criticized both Democrats and Republicans.

Her most prominent political issue in recent years has become the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Her outspoken support for Palestinians and criticism of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza have also produced significant controversy in Hollywood.

Susan Sarandon and Donald Trump

Sarandon did not endorse Donald Trump in the 2016 election.

Instead, she supported Bernie Sanders during the Democratic primary. After Sanders lost the nomination, Sarandon did not support Hillary Clinton and instead endorsed Green Party presidential candidate Jill Stein. The Hollywood Reporter reported her Stein endorsement in November 2016.

Her comments about Trump during the 2016 campaign were nevertheless controversial.

Sarandon argued that Trump’s election could potentially help create the political conditions for a progressive backlash. She also criticized Clinton and expressed strong reservations about supporting the Democratic nominee.

But that position should not be converted into the claim that Sarandon was a Trump supporter. She was a critic of the Democratic establishment who believed that Clinton’s politics, particularly on foreign policy, represented a serious problem.

In an April 2016 interview, Sarandon explicitly said she did not support Trump while sharply criticizing Clinton.

That distinction is important when describing her politics today.

Sarandon’s progressive and anti-war politics

Sarandon’s activism predates Trump by decades.

She has been associated with:

opposition to the Iraq War;
progressive economic causes;
women’s and civil-rights issues;
criticism of corporate political influence;
the Occupy Wall Street movement;
Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaigns;
opposition to U.S. military intervention;
Palestinian rights and criticism of U.S. policy toward Israel.

Her politics have therefore frequently placed her to the left of the Democratic Party establishment.

Sarandon, Israel and Palestine

The issue that has generated the greatest recent controversy around Sarandon is her outspoken support for Palestinians.

In 2023, she appeared at pro-Palestinian demonstrations following the Hamas attack on Israel and the beginning of the Gaza war. Some of her comments were widely condemned as offensive and antisemitic.

United Talent Agency dropped Sarandon as a client in November 2023 after comments she made at a pro-Palestinian rally. UTA confirmed the decision, according to reporting by the Los Angeles Times, Variety and other outlets.

Sarandon subsequently apologized for some of her remarks and said she regretted causing pain to the Jewish community.

What Sarandon says now

At the 2026 Venice Film Festival, Sarandon said she was still losing acting opportunities because of her political activism.

Reuters reported on Sept. 6 that Sarandon said she had recently lost film roles because some agencies were telling producers not to hire her. She attributed the problem particularly to her criticism of Israel and support for Palestinians.

She was in Venice promoting The Echo Chamber, directed by Andrea Pallaoro. Reuters reported that Sarandon thanked Pallaoro for casting her despite warnings from people in the industry.

The episode illustrates the unusual position Sarandon occupies in Hollywood: she remains firmly associated with the political left, but her views on Israel, Palestine and U.S. foreign policy have put her at odds with parts of the entertainment establishment.

Actors Who Have Openly Supported Donald Trump

Hollywood remains overwhelmingly Democratic, but a group of actors have publicly supported Trump, including some who have become prominent conservative voices.

Jon Voight is one of Trump’s most prominent Hollywood supporters.

Voight has repeatedly defended Trump publicly and endorsed his presidential campaigns. Trump appointed Voight, Mel Gibson and Sylvester Stallone as special ambassadors to Hollywood in 2025.

Gibson publicly supported Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign. His support subsequently became more visible after Trump returned to the White House.

Trump included Gibson among the three Hollywood figures he designated as special ambassadors to the industry in 2025.

Sylvester Stallone

Stallone is another major Hollywood name who publicly backed Trump.

In November 2024, Stallone introduced Trump at a gala and compared the president-elect to a “second George Washington.” The Hollywood Reporter documented the remarks.

Trump later appointed Stallone as one of his Hollywood special ambassadors.

Dennis Quaid

Quaid openly endorsed Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign and spoke publicly about his support.

Forbes identified Quaid among the actors who endorsed Trump before the 2024 election.

Zachary Levi

Levi publicly endorsed Trump in 2024 after initially describing himself as politically independent.

His endorsement was one of the more notable examples of a younger Hollywood actor breaking with the industry’s dominant Democratic political culture. Forbes listed him among Trump’s celebrity supporters.

Kelsey Grammer

The Frasier star has repeatedly acknowledged his support for Trump.

In a 2023 BBC interview, Grammer was asked whether he still supported Trump. His answer was yes. The interview subsequently became controversial when the discussion of his politics was reportedly cut short by representatives.

James Woods

Woods is one of the most outspoken Trump supporters in Hollywood.

He has repeatedly used social media to defend Trump and attack his political opponents. Deadline described Woods as a “vocal Trump supporter” during the 2024 campaign.

Drea de Matteo

The Sopranos actress became an outspoken MAGA supporter.

In 2024, de Matteo publicly discussed her support for Trump and said she believed many Hollywood figures privately supported him even if they did not say so publicly. Variety reported extensively on her political shift.

Other documented Trump-supporting actors

Other actors who have publicly endorsed or supported Trump include:

Roseanne Barr
Stephen Baldwin

Jim Caviezel
Robert Davi
Kristy Swanson
Kevin Sorbo
John Schneider
Rob Schneider
Antonio Sabàto Jr.
Nick Searcy
Isaiah Washington
Vince Vaughn

The level of political involvement varies considerably among these actors. Some have simply endorsed Trump, while others have become regular conservative political voices.

Actors Who Have Been Openly Critical of Trump

The list of Hollywood actors who have criticized Trump is considerably larger.

Robert De Niro

De Niro is among Trump’s most outspoken celebrity critics.

During the 2024 campaign, he appeared outside Trump’s New York criminal trial and warned voters about a second Trump presidency. AP reported extensively on the confrontation between De Niro and Trump supporters outside the courthouse.

De Niro has continued to criticize Trump publicly.

George Clooney

Clooney has long supported Democratic candidates and was a major fundraiser for Joe Biden in 2024.

In 2026, Clooney has remained sharply critical of the Trump administration. At the Venice Film Festival in September, he criticized the current political climate and expressed hope that the 2026 midterm elections would provide a check on the administration.

Mark Ruffalo

Ruffalo has consistently opposed Trump and supported progressive causes.

Following Trump’s 2024 election victory, Ruffalo spoke publicly about the political situation and remained active in progressive advocacy.

In 2026, he has also become a prominent critic of corporate and political involvement in the Israel-Palestine conflict.

Meryl Streep

Streep has been one of Trump’s most prominent Hollywood critics.

Her 2017 Golden Globes speech, delivered shortly before Trump took office, became one of the defining examples of Hollywood opposition to the incoming president.

Julia Roberts

Roberts supported Biden in 2024 and participated in the major Democratic fundraising effort featuring Barack Obama, George Clooney and other Hollywood figures. AP reported on the event and the participation of major Hollywood donors.

Other prominent Trump critics

Actors and entertainers who have publicly criticized Trump or supported his Democratic opponents include:

Jamie Lee Curtis
Mark Hamill
Leonardo DiCaprio
Jennifer Lawrence
Samuel L. Jackson
John Leguizamo
Jeffrey Wright
America Ferrera
Pedro Pascal
Alyssa Milano
Patricia Arquette
Viola Davis
Will Ferrell
Harrison Ford

For the 2024 election, numerous major actors publicly backed Joe Biden or Kamala Harris. Forbes noted that actors including Viola Davis, Dick Van Dyke, Will Ferrell, Harrison Ford and Leonardo DiCaprio were among the prominent Hollywood figures supporting Harris, while Trump’s publicly declared Hollywood support remained comparatively small.

Susan Sarandon vs. Hollywood’s Trump Supporters

The political distinction is important.

news.title: PRedictions, PRojections, PRaise, and PRedators: Just a Boy and His Colon
news.text:
Stuck in both ends: Suddenly, I felt great empathy for an ear of corn — and I’ll never look at corn holders the same way.

(I also made sure the doc was going to use different tubes. Because, eww.)

Obviously, a colonoscopy is a deeply humbling procedure. You’re vulnerable. Everything about it is utterly humiliating, including your trip to the local pharmacy for your “liquid bowel prep.” 

By the way, aren’t pharmacists with super-loud voices awesome? Thanks, babe. Thanks for sharing with the room while ringing me up.

Then she asked me if I wanted a plastic bag. I said, “No thanks, I’m gonna wait ‘til I go home to take it.” (Long story short, I’m not allowed in that pharmacy anymore.)

So, yeah — not a fun week. But y’know what? 

I don’t regret being an ear of corn.

Because what’s far worse than a colonoscopy is dying from something preventable.

Most roadmaps aren’t linear. There are twists and turns. Construction and offramps. Stormy days and unexpected detours.

And sometimes, you’ve got to take a step backward before you can go forward.

In pro sports, there are two theories on momentum. The first is that momentum is a precious commodity — and the team that has it will continue to have it unless it’s forcefully taken away. Ex-Dallas Cowboys and Miami Dolphins Hall of Fame head coach Jimmy Johnson was a true believer and would call plays specifically to swing momentum.

The second theory says the opposite: The past is the past; don’t be superstitious. In the words of Baltimore Orioles Hall of Fame manager Earl Weaver, “Momentum is only as good as tomorrow’s starting pitcher.”

In politics, both theories are true.

Momentum will hurt Republicans in the 2026 midterms. After riding high in 2024, the Dems regained momentum in most of the high-profile off-year elections, including the governorships in Virginia and New Jersey. Since then, the Dems have (generally) outperformed Republicans.

Energy and momentum are all on their side. In today’s culture, outrage is the opiate of the masses — and the Democratic base has been slurping it by the barrelful. They’re energized and mobilized.

This matters in 2026, because public sentiment is like the ocean’s tides: Sometimes it’s high, sometimes it’s low. 

Right now, for the GOP, it’s low. The Democrats own the inside track.

If the current trajectory holds, the Republicans will almost certainly lose the House — and the Senate isn’t any better than a coin flip. (Go check out the odds for yourself. It ain’t looking good.)

Newtonian physics also applies to politics: “An object in motion tends to stay in motion.” That means momentum is a force of its own. And it’ll continue to be a force — unless and until there’s a paradigm shift.

So, it seems, Jimmy Johnson’s theory is correct…

…right until it isn’t.

Because that’s the political paradox. It’s where Johnson’s theory ends and Weaver’s takes over: Winning big in November is itself a paradigm shift. 

And paradigm shifts will swing momentum in unpredictable ways. They always do.

Suddenly, it’s a brand-new ball game.

If the Democrats win the midterms, there’ll be new faces on TV, new men and women in leadership roles, and new “brand ambassadors” for the Democratic Party. 

Including, very possibly, Abdul El-Sayed. 

After all, when the messengers change, so does the message. Can’t change one without the other. In tone, timing, and substance, it’s going to be different.

Which basically means, the Dems are gonna have new starting pitchers.

I hate losing. And I really, REALLY hate losing when the players are playing their hearts out — but bad management and/or bad coaching costs them the win. Getting obliterated because the other team was simply better is one thing; losing a winnable game is maddening.

Despite all the chaos of the Iran War, gas prices, and historic headwinds, I still believe the 2026 midterms are winnable for the GOP — but only if we’re smarter and more disciplined than the Dems. We need, to paraphrase Bret “The Hitman” Hart, “excellence in execution.”

Unfortunately, I don’t see the GOP’s messaging coalescing. Everything is still too scattered.

And it’s far from excellent.

Now, we’re starting to run out of time. Things need to escalate in a hurry, or else…

… we might win EVERYTHING in 2028.

PRediction: Hate to say it, but the best thing for the GOP’s 2028 chances is losing in 2026.

Republican PR works better against a foil. When it’s us versus perfection, the media has a free hand to hang every imperfection over our heads. The Democrats will promise a “free this” and a “free that” ‘til the cows come home. Meanwhile, the GOP is responsible for explaining the status quo.

When the status quo falls out of favor, that’s a big disadvantage.

But once the Dems own the end product, this dynamic changes. Suddenly, they have skin in the game, too. They’re no longer spectators; they’re part of the circus. (Clowns, usually.)

And instead of comparing Republicans with perfection, voters will compare Republicans with Democrats.

If the Dems win the House, they’ll spend the next two years harassing Donald Trump’s family. There’ll be bogus investigations, impeachment hearings, and pointless fishing expeditions. Pinheads in Congress will swarm to CNN and MS NOW, tossing juicy morsels of red meat tofu to their Democratic Socialist base.

The crazier — and the more extreme — the Democrats act, the better it’ll be for the Republicans in 2028.

It’s like the old joke about two middle-aged dudes in the African savannah: Suddenly, a lion charges forward. The first guy takes off, huffing and puffing away.

“Are you crazy?!” yelled his friend. “A lion can run 50 miles per hour! You can’t outrun a lion!”

“I don’t need to outrun the lion,” the other friend replied, “I just need to outrun you.”

PRojection: This doesn’t mean the 2026 midterms are unwinnable — or that we shouldn’t try to win.

It means we desperately need to shift momentum somehow, and if the end result is that we won’t have left-wing loons in the House to scare the [EXPLETIVE] out of Flyover Country in the run-up to 2028, so be it.

Hey, if we end up winning a low-tide election in 2026, it stands to reason we could also do it in 2028.

Besides, an awful lot of voters are apolitical. Politics isn’t on their day-to-day radar. They follow it like it’s the WNBA: Yeah, they’ve heard of Caitlin Clark (and think Sophie Cunningham is flippin’ adorable), but 99.99% of the time when you ask ‘em about it, they’re echoing what other people are saying instead of watching the games themselves. 

Their “opinions” are mostly regurgitations. They’re loosely aware of the major storylines, but that’s about it.

Post-Labor Day is when apolitical voters begin to pay attention — and develop opinions of their own. 

And even though the Dems have the momentum, the GOP has the money. WAY more money.

And maybe, momentum can be purchased.

PRaise: The GOP’s challenge is: How can we use our money advantage to swing the momentum in 2026?

Big praise to all the Republican donors, by the way. (If you were one of ‘em, you rock!) In our pay-to-play world, the bottom line is: money makes messages go farther. Used correctly, money can elevate awareness, mobilize voters, and energize your base for Election Day.

And used incorrectly, you can set your whole dang pile of money on fire. (See Kamala Harris, circa 2024.)

Money is an asset, but it’s up to the spender to use it wisely. Results aren’t guaranteed.

My advice for the GOP: Develop a transparent “metrics dashboard” that’s shared with high-ranking campaign officials. Relevant metrics would include polling data, ad buys, social media engagement, candidate fundraising, and anything else that can be tracked and quantified.

Don’t spend your money blindly. Develop a strategy, test the results — and when the metrics jump positively, double down and spend more.

That’s how you swing momentum!

Because, if you waste donors’ money, it won’t just sink us in the midterms. The consequences will have longer legs, I’m afraid.

It’ll also demotivate donors from cutting a check in 2028, too. (See Democratic Party, circa 2026.)

PRedator: “See what became of him today, the predator became the prey.”

Thought experiment: If the “worst thing” happens — and the GOP shocks the world by winning the midterms — what should our next strategic PR move be?

In other words, what happens if we get to go on offense instead of defense?

Yes, we’d lose the Dems as our House-controlling, overreaching, impeachment-obsessed foils, but we’d also inherit a Democratic Party that’s on the verge of a nervous breakdown: After losing to Trump in 2024, if they lose the 2026 midterms too, left-wing heads will explode! Every Dem will be frothing mad!

Which means, the Democrats will be pointing fingers and tearing each other to shreds.

And that’s fine for us. Let the circular firing squad commence: Ready, aim, fire!

If this happens, our next move is obvious: Split the Dems into two parties — a liberal party and a socialist party — and keep ‘em in a permanent minority for the foreseeable future.

Wouldn’t that be great? The Dems divided; the Republicans united. All our problems would be behind us.

(Hey! Just like a colonoscopy!)

news.title: 'Lanterns' Goes Back to Hollywood's Woke Well
news.text:
Suffice it to say we won't be seeing "Eternals 2" or more "Marvels" anytime soon.

So the MCU course corrected. It brought back Chris Evans to play Captain America once more, replacing Anthony Mackie who briefly played the star-spangled hero. The series ditched the woke warriors and played up the nostalgia element with this December's "Avengers: Doomsday." 

The upcoming films find both Cap and Thor (Chris Hemsworth) as new parents, and their battles to protect humanity have a deeply human element — the nuclear-ish family.

Tell this to James Gunn's DC universe.

The saga's newest entry, HBO Max's "Lanterns," feels like it was air-dropped from the Peak Woke era — think the 2020 Summer of Love.

The show, starring Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler, follows the classic Green Lanterns saga, at least on paper. Except something seemed off from the start. First, a critical white character died in the pilot episode.

Next, said character was retconned to be a cranky, egotistical jerk. It felt like "The Last Jedi's" Luke Skywalker syndrome all over again, turning a classic hero into someone you wouldn't sit next to at a BBQ. 

Next, some of the show's talents woked up the joint in promotional interviews, extolling what a better world we'd have if only Vice President Kamala Harris had been the president.

Here's co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson sharing how America doesn't trust black women based on the results of one election. (He didn't mention Jasmine Crockett ... hmmm.)

Could you imagine where we would be right now if Kamala got up in there, dog? Could you imagine how it would’ve been? It’d be a lot different. So we’re experiencing the consequences of not trusting a black woman.

What a way to pitch a TV series.

And there's the show itself. The latest episodes feature full-on lectures about racism in America. The speeches sound like someone from 2026, but the chronology of the show is all over the map. The following quote was uttered in 2016. Here's the wife of a wealthy militia leader attacking both her husband and white people in toto.

White men have the privilege of being eccentric. White men with money? They can do whatever the f*** they want. Play cowboy, build castles.

Episode three doubles down on the race-based lectures. Here, the mother of Aaron Pierre's John Stewart character gives a speech on being black in America in the 1990s.

Do you understand how unfair it is to ask a Black man in America if he’s afraid?” We are terrified daily of persecution and still show up, sometimes better than everyone around us. Did you know that?

Woke or not, "Lanterns" arrives with a distinct advantage. It's much easier, and cheaper to watch the show than see a woke movie. The barriers to entry for woke TV are far easier than their theatrical peers.

The early ratings for the show are strong. Now, imagine if the series had respected the source material and kept the lectures off screen. That's not to say a show can't touch on race, but the way "Lanterns" is handling the subject feels like Woke Storytelling 101. 

The show could be a blockbuster, but Gunn's DC universe would rather lecture than entertain.

news.title: Without Charlie Kirk, Turning Point is building a future for his movement — and for JD Vance
news.text:
Charlie Kirk sat before a Salt Lake City audience of restaurateurs last September 10, dispensing business advice drawn from his own unlikely rise.

The conservative activist argued that a company needed a deep connection to the founder’s “energy and vision” to endure, but he also warned that “separating the brand from the founder” was among the greatest challenges an entrepreneur could face.

“We have not done this successfully yet,” Kirk acknowledged of Turning Point USA, the organization he built to influence and mobilize young people.

Hours later, a gunman fatally shot Kirk on a Utah college campus. He was 31.

In the year since his death, Turning Point’s leaders — including Kirk’s widow, Erika, and some of his closest friends and lieutenants — have confronted the very challenge he described that tragic morning: preserving and expanding a political movement that had been built, to an extraordinary degree, around the energy, instincts and celebrity of its charismatic leader.

They have done so amid remarkable circumstances, including the criminal case against Kirk’s alleged killer; conservative influencers warring over his legacy; and far-right figures, led by former Turning Point employee Candace Owens, spreading baseless conspiracy theories about his death.

The 2026 midterm elections present the biggest test yet of the question hanging over the organization: What is Turning Point without Charlie Kirk?

“There is a void, and lots of people are trying to fill it,” Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters told CNN, “but no one will be able to do what he did.”

By some measures, the answer is a larger organization than the one Kirk left behind. About 1,500 colleges have Turning Point chapters on campus, up 64% over the past year, according to an internal document obtained by CNN, and affiliated high school clubs have nearly tripled. Turning Point now says it has over 1 million donors and more than 1,200 employees.

Its political operation is expanding, too. Turning Point staff and volunteers are embedded in more states with contests critical to Republican power in 2026 — and the presidential race two years later.

The stakes extend to the political ambitions of Vice President JD Vance, a close Kirk friend whom the organization has already endorsed for president in 2028. Whether the organization can sustain Kirk’s movement — and mobilize the voters he spent years courting — could help determine whether the vice president can inherit the political coalition Donald Trump assembled.

“If you believe in JD that much, that’s even more motivation to work our butts off and throw the kitchen sink at this thing,” said Tyler Bowyer, the chief operating officer for Turning Point Action. “We’re going to do everything we possibly can to win (in 2026) because so much is at stake — in this case, getting JD to run.”

Turning Point’s own effectiveness, though, has come under scrutiny in its home state, Arizona, where some Republicans fault the polarizing organization for the party’s recent electoral defeats. This year, the group has put its muscle behind Rep. Andy Biggs, a conservative Trump ally whose candidacy for governor has revived anxieties about hard-right nominees who narrowly lost statewide races.

Meanwhile, the political coalition Turning Point helped build faces new strains largely beyond the organization’s control. Polls show that young voters, whose sharp shift toward Trump in 2024 further elevated Kirk’s stature within the party, have soured on the president.

Turning Point spokesman Andrew Kolvet acknowledged the movement is facing headwinds, “and that’s especially true among young voters.”

“They are telling us they are worried about housing, affordability, foreign policy, etc.,” Kolvet said. “But if anyone has the political talent and ability to address their needs, wants and concerns directly ahead of the midterms, it’s President Trump and JD Vance.”

Finding Kirk’s voice

Kirk founded Turning Point USA in 2012 at age 18. What began as a nonprofit for young conservatives eventually grew into a sprawling, multimillion-dollar network that touched all aspects of American politics, including faith, culture, schools, voter registration, candidate endorsements and campaign fundraising.

But Turning Point also served as a massive platform for Kirk himself. His podcast and viral confrontations with liberals on college campuses made him one of the right’s most visible personalities, while his relationships across the movement bridged some of the divides within Trump’s MAGA coalition.

That part of Turning Point has proved difficult to replace.

Clips from Kirk’s podcast, now hosted by Kolvet, rarely draw the YouTube audiences they once did. Others have tried, with mixed success, to re-create the virality of his campus debates. And the right-wing online ecosystem where Kirk served as connective tissue between competing factions has frayed during Trump’s second term.

Turning Point’s leaders privately acknowledge there is no replacing Kirk, who will be honored one year after his death at Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday. Instead, they have focused on what they can preserve and expand: the organization he built around himself.

“Yes, we don’t have Charlie’s social media anymore, which is a big loss. And we don’t have his voice — huge deal,” a person involved in the organization told CNN. “But the actual machinery of Turning Point has never been bigger.”

As evidence, they pointed to a recent training for 150 new staffers. Online job boards show dozens of openings to work for Turning Point in battleground states.

“We’re going to be even bigger this election than we were in 2024,” Bowyer said.

Turning Point’s Super Bowl

Political memorabilia adorns the shelves of Bowyer’s office — a Calvin Coolidge pendant, a bust of Teddy Roosevelt, and a framed print of Newsweek’s never-published 2016 “Madam President” cover of Hillary Clinton next to Time’s cover featuring Trump as Person of the Year.

Among them is a painting of Kirk, whose face is inescapable throughout Turning Point’s Arizona campus.

There, Bowyer oversees the organization’s voter turnout machine — the “pinnacle” of Kirk’s legacy, as he described it.

“It’s kind of like the Super Bowl,” Bowyer said. “It’s pointless to educate hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of young people, for them just to go, ‘Oh, you know, don’t use that.’ Right?”

He added, “Charlie really believes in that,” slipping into present tense to describe his deceased friend and former leader — not for the only time during a 90-minute interview with CNN.

Bowyer is now expanding a program piloted in the 2024 election. Then, the group embedded staff and volunteers in neighborhoods throughout Arizona to mobilize potential Republican voters. Rather than send canvassers to knock on as many doors as possible, Turning Point instructed its organizers to make genuine connections, build relationships, show up at local events and, at least initially, avoid talking politics.

It’s a strategy built around quality, not quantity, Bowyer argues.

By Election Day, organizers are expected to have a plan for getting their assigned households — about 600 to 1,000 people — to the polls or to vote by mail. “Ballot chasers” are tasked with ensuring they follow through. Each organizer’s goal is to turn out about half their designated voters — a much higher threshold than traditional canvassers.

The effectiveness of the operation is difficult to measure, and there are Republican skeptics, including within Trump’s own political operation. But Turning Point emerged from 2024 with a compelling result to point to: Trump won Arizona by 5.5 percentage points, his largest victory of all the battleground states.

The victory emboldened Turning Point to double down in 2026. Even before the midterm map had fully taken shape, the organization was deploying staff and hiring in key battleground states. Maps of those states line the walls inside Turning Point Action’s headquarters with heat maps of voters and detailed breakdowns on “chaseable votes.”

This spring, the operation had a dry run when it joined the White House’s retribution campaign against Republican lawmakers in Indiana who resisted Trump’s calls to redraw the state’s congressional boundaries. Trump-backed challengers defeated seven of the eight GOP holdouts.

Indiana Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith, a Trump ally, said Turning Point mobilized quickly despite little history in his state and noted the group left behind manpower for future political battles.

“The proof is in the pudding. Critics could say, ‘This is the first year. What good are they going to do?’” Beckwith said. “I don’t know how you break down the pie chart of who deserves credit, but we won and won in a big way.”

Republican operatives in key states say Turning Point is already making its presence felt. Former New Hampshire GOP Chairman Chris Ager said the group arrived on the ground far earlier than usual for a grassroots organization, hired experienced local activists and their visibility has been “extremely high.”

Jason Roe, a veteran Michigan strategist, said Turning Point’s organizers have been more “engaged and impactful” than the college-age men and women he typically encounters in groups for young Republican.

“Turning Point is made up of true believers,” Roe said. “They’re griding because they care, not because it’s the first step on a journey to getting involved in politics.”

In Iowa, Turning Point’s growing influence has already been tested against the most powerful endorsement in Republican politics.

The organization supported businessman and farmer Zach Lahn in the state’s closely watched Republican primary for governor. Trump backed Rep. Randy Feenstra.

“We were so busy talking about the Trump endorsement,” said Jeff Angelo, a prominent conservative radio host in Iowa, “that we missed the most important endorsement: Turning Point Action.”

Trouble in the desert

No one needs less convincing of Turning Point’s sway with GOP voters than Julie Spilsbury.

Last year, Bowyer made it his stated mission to oust Spilsbury, a registered Republican who supported Kamala Harris for president over Trump, from the City Council in Mesa, where he resides. Turning Point helped lead an effort to recall her, and in December 2025, Spilsbury lost the seat she had held for five years by about 700 votes.

“It was devastating and heartbreaking and made a lot of people mad,” she said.

Spilsbury considers herself a casualty of Turning Point’s growing clout in the Arizona GOP — and what she and others described as its vindictive approach to intraparty politics. The organization has aggressively intervened in primaries and endorsed dozens of candidates, stacking up wins and bruising fellow Republicans along the way.

The clashes have become increasingly public. Bowyer faced blowback in July after he questioned on X whether Arizona state Rep. Quang Nguyen, a Republican who escaped communist Vietnam as a child, can speak English. When Republican state Rep. Nick Kupper came to Nguyen’s defense, Bowyer threatened to back a challenger against Kupper in 2028 and later announced Turning Point was withdrawing its endorsement.

Reached by CNN via email, Kupper declined to revisit the episode. Attempts to reach Nguyen through his office were unsuccessful.

Such tactics might go overlooked by Republicans in the Trump era if Turning Point was consistently turning its primary success into general election wins. In Arizona, it has not.

The organization played a key role in the unsuccessful 2022 campaigns of Republican gubernatorial nominee Kari Lake and GOP Senate candidate Blake Masters. Lake lost a Senate race two years later.

A Turning Point official noted the organization didn’t endorse Lake in her primaries but jumped in to help after she became the GOP nominee. Still, Bowyer contended they were “on the path for Kari to win” in 2022. The lesson from the loss, he argued, was that the organization needed more manpower.

“If we would have kept going and chased more votes, I think we could have won,” he said. Lake lost the governor’s race by roughly 17,000 votes.

The defeats have spread to far smaller Arizona contests. Earlier this year, Turning Point jumped into races for the Salt River Project, a local utility board whose elections typically draw little public attention. The group’s involvement drove a surge in turnout from both sides, but clean-energy candidates ultimately won a majority of seats for the first time in recent memory.

The Turning Point official argued that the group secured the two most critical positions leading the board “amid national headwinds that have impacted local races.” But progressives claimed victory after the election, and even local Republicans have acknowledged the board’s leftward turn was a significant setback.

“I think (Turning Point) is bombing hard, and it’s excellent for everyone else. I hesitate to say too much because we don’t want them to stop,” said Autumn Johnson, executive director of the Arizona Solar Energy Industries Association. “They have absolutely no idea what they’re doing, and they don’t know they don’t know what they’re doing. And it turns out a lot of people hate them.”

Their presence is causing divisions within the GOP at a time when the party is losing power across the state, argued Nick Myers, a member of the Arizona Corporation Commission, a state utility board. A Turning Point-backed challenger defeated Myers in a primary earlier this year. He said he lost the organization’s support after a back-and-forth on X with Bowyer a few years ago.

“As soon as they started getting involved, Republicans started losing,” Myers said. “It’s not because we’re becoming a purple state. Voters can’t stand the candidates Turning Point is nominating. Their days are limited if they don’t start putting up candidates who can win.”

The organization is betting on Biggs, the gubernatorial nominee, to reverse the party’s recent fortunes. The Turning Point official noted that Biggs was one of Kirk’s final and most passionate endorsements, viewing him as “a transformational and generational leader for Arizona — somebody who could turn Arizona into the Florida of the West.”

Bowyer said Biggs is a more seasoned politician than his predecessors and is better positioned to take on Katie Hobbs, the nation’s most vulnerable Democratic governor this year. Turning Point is now more experienced in campaign work, too, he added.

Some Republicans in Arizona view the race as a referendum on Turning Point as much as Biggs. Barrett Marson, a longtime GOP operative in Arizona, said if Biggs wins, many Republicans expect Turning Point to effectively take over the state GOP. A loss, though, would have its own consequences.

“Turning Point is all in on two people: Andy Biggs and JD Vance,” Marson said. “If both of those guys lose their upcoming elections, I predict they won’t be around much after 2028.”

Vance-Turning Point 2028?

Turning Point recently doubled its staff in Iowa and is rapidly deploying organizers in New Hampshire ahead of key midterm races in both states. When the elections are over, the teams will remain — and wait for Vance to make a decision.

Erika Kirk sent one of the first shockwaves through the 2028 presidential race in December when she endorsed Vance — getting ahead not only of the vice president, but of Trump, who is widely expected to play a decisive role in choosing his successor. Since then, Turning Point has set out to demonstrate that a turnkey organization will be waiting for Vance if he launches a White House bid.

Ager, the former New Hampshire party chairman, said Turning Point could present a “significant organizational advantage out of the gate” for Vance in 2028 when Republicans there vote in the GOP’s first presidential primary. Iowa, meanwhile, will hold the party’s first nominating contest.

“It’s still up to the candidate to convince voters,” he said. “But a good organization absolutely helps.”

Vance has remained close to Turning Point, appearing at several events and guest-hosting Kirk’s podcast.

The mutual loyalty is “downstream of the genuine close friendship that JD had with Charlie,” a source close to the vice president told CNN. Kirk helped propel Vance within the party and into his current role.

Though he remains reticent to publicly discuss his political future, Vance privately views Turning Point’s support as a key to his future ambitions, the source said. The organization offers Vance a connection to “America First” stalwarts in Trump’s coalition and a well-funded political infrastructure separate from the president’s political operation.

“They are specifically a MAGA power center, versus a traditional power center,” the source said. “They are distinctly different from the old guard establishment that wouldn’t necessarily support JD, and that serves as a true home for the MAGA voters.”

Bowyer said he expects Vance to closely watch the midterm results before he finalizes his plans. But he added, “If people want you to run, and you decide not to run, you usually don’t ever get a chance to run again.”

For Turning Point, delivering Republican victories this fall, particularly in Arizona, would give Vance reason to trust the organization Kirk left behind could help carry him to the White House.

Failure would bring its own reckoning, and Bowyer said Turning Point would judge itself more harshly than any outside critic if the group fell short.

Said Bowyer: “Charlie felt that way.”
