news.text:
A rush transcript of "This Week with George Stephanopoulos" airing on Sunday, September 6, 2026 on ABC News is below. This copy may not be in its final form, may be updated and may contain minor transcription errors. For previous show transcripts, visit the "This Week" transcript archive.

MARTHA RADDATZ, ABC “THIS WEEK” CO-ANCHOR: The U.S. and Iran trade attacks in the Strait, as Americans face record high gas prices for Labor Day.

“THIS WEEK” starts right now.

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

RADDATZ: What war? Into the war’s seventh month, President Trump downplays it.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us. It’s not a big thing.

RADDATZ: All as Americans feel the pain as gas and diesel prices soar.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It’s scary. Honestly, I just pulled up and I didn’t expect to see $4.57 for regular gas right now.

RADDATZ: This morning, we speak with Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

Turmoil at the Pentagon.

VICE ADM. NANCY LACORE, FORMER CHIEF OF U.S. NAVY RESERVE (RET.) & (D) SOUTH CAROLINA CONGRESSIONAL CANDIDATE: You know, it’s just weakening our military and really putting our country at risk.

RADDATZ: After the Army secretary resigns, growing concerns over Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s leadership.

REP. DON BACON, (R) NEBRASKA: He would not be on my team.

RADDATZ: Former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall with his warnings over the state of the military.

A plea for civility.

GOV. SPENCER COX, (R) UTAH: Seventy percent of this country doesn’t like where we are right now. They’re tired of the hyper partisanship.

RADDATZ: One year after Charlie Kirk’s assassination, we speak with Utah Governor Spencer Cox about his new book on “Off Ramp,” and his push to turn down the temperature.

Plus, 25 years later.

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I was not alive for 9/11.

JAY O'BRIEN, ABC NEWS CORRESPONDENT: What do you know about it?

RADDATZ: The college class trying to preserve the memory of 9/11 for a new generation.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

ANNOUNCER: From ABC News it’s “THIS WEEK.” Here now, Martha Raddatz.

RADDATZ: Good morning and welcome to “THIS WEEK” on this Labor Day weekend. A weekend where gas prices are rising and so are tensions in the Middle East. We are now into the war’s seventh month, despite President Trump calling it small potatoes and the vice president refusing to even call it a war. It has flared up once again.

On Saturday, Iran launching ballistic missiles at a U.S. Navy destroyer and an aircraft carrier. The U.S. firing back, disabling or destroying three Iranian oil tankers. That, of course, in addition to the fact we have had 18 Americans killed and nearly 800 wounded.

And with just 58 days until the midterms, voters are watching this all play out, the Iran war, the rising price of gas and the state of the Trump presidency in general.

Our Rachel Scott was watching it all from the White House this week and leads us off.

(BEGIN VIDEOTAPE)

RACHEL SCOTT, ABC NEWS SENIOR POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT (voice over): Into the Iran War’s seventh month with no end in sight, President Trump declaring this week the conflict is, quote, “small potatoes.”

SCOTT: Can you explain to the American people, if this is not a war, what exactly is it?

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Well, I’ll tell you what, a lot of people don’t call it a war. I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us. It’s not a big thing.

SCOTT (voice over): But 18 U.S. service members have died, nearly 800 have been wounded, in a conflict the president said would only last four to six weeks.

SCOTT: It certainly doesn’t feel like small potatoes. Eighteen service members have died. We’re seeing record long deployments. You initially said this would last --

TRUMP: Record long -- why is it record long? So --

SCOTT: Well, the 82nd Airborne is now being extended to a year.

TRUMP: How long are we in Vietnam? How long were we in Vietnam?

SCOTT: We’re seeing record --

TRUMP: No, no, how long were we in Vietnam?

SCOTT: The USS Abraham Lincoln was out for more than 250 days at sea.

TRUMP: We’re in five months now.

SCOTT (voice over): The president making those comments as he defended Vice President J.D. Vance, who earlier in the week claimed it was not a war.

J.D. VANCE, VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I wouldn’t call it a war. Right now there is no active shooting.

SCOTT (voice over): This week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick issued an apology after he says he misspoke when he forgot those 18 Americans who have died.

HOWARD LUTNICK, COMMERCE SECRETARY: I think the way the president is playing Iran, right, there’s not -- there haven’t been American deaths. It’s really just an economic choke out, which the administration is now executing more broadly.

SCOTT (voice over): Lutnick later saying he was thinking about the operation in Venezuela.

But by Saturday morning, the two sides trading attacks again. U.S. forces striking three Iranian crude oil carriers responding to Iran launching ballistic missiles toward two U.S. Navy warships.

CENTCOM Commander Brad Cooper saying in a statement, “if you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost, taking out three of yours.”

Meanwhile, President Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, and son-in-law Jared Kushner in Moscow yesterday, pushing for an end to the war in Ukraine. A White House official tells ABC News, the two discussed substantive plans for the next steps and a plan for peace. The pair arriving in Ukraine this morning to meet with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

It comes as Vladimir Putin has increased his assault on Kyiv, striking the Ukrainian capital at a level not seen since the earliest days of the war.

Ukraine ramping up their own attacks, hammering Russian energy infrastructure and striking deeper into Russian territory.

SCOTT BESSENT, TREASURY SECRETARY: We are going through an energy shock right now due to both the war in Ukraine, because, you know, Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets and refined products. So, that is creating upward price pressure on a global basis.

(END VIDEOTAPE)

SCOTT (on camera): So, Martha, back to the war with Iran. Clearly, the larger problem for the Trump administration is the backup in the Strait of Hormuz. This war has no end in sight, and the conflict is driving up gas prices, Martha.

RADDATZ: Thanks, Rachel.

I'm joined now by the secretary of Energy, Chris Wright.

Good morning, Mr. Secretary.

As you know, we have renewed fighting with Iran. In fact, Iran is claiming they hit some ships overnight. President Trump has called this “small potatoes,” but it seems like we are still at war.

ENERGY SECRETARY CHRIS WRIGHT: Look, it's a challenge. Iran is doing everything they can to cling on to something. They know their nuclear program's coming to an end. Their navy has come to an end. Their air force has come to an end.

They're clinging on to power as the United States continues to escalate the volume of oil that transits through the Strait of Hormuz. And when you add it together with the bypass pipelines, we're at two-thirds or so of total pre-conflict transits. And the world's had some buffers to not completely, but mostly offset that. So, things aren't looking so good for Iran.

RADDATZ: But would you say we're still at war? They did hit -- they did launch ballistic missiles.

WRIGHT: We're still in a conflict, for sure. The United States Navy is there to reduce Iran's ability to cause trouble, but they're doing everything they can to cause trouble. And the United States' capabilities to deflect that have continued to grow. But we're in a conflict zone.

RADDATZ: You said that Monday we broke a wartime record with 17 million barrels a day passing through. The average before the war was 20 million barrels a day. Have we sustained that this week? What was our seven-day average?

WRIGHT: The seven-day average right now is a little over nine million barrels a day, which is the highest the seven-day average has ever been. So, it continues to migrate up. And then there's also the bypass pipelines through Saudi Arabia, through the United Arab Emirates. And when you add those together, the flow through the -- out of that region is more like 13 million, 14 million barrels a day.

RADDATZ: You also said, and just now again, that Iran is losing its ability to hold the world economic hostage. You talk about our troops being there. We have 50,000 troops being there. They are certainly escorting -- helping to escort these ships.

How long can we sustain that? Do we have to have that to maintain this?

WRIGHT: Well, we'd love to see help from allies in the region, and I suspect we'll see some of that. But the critical mission that our Navy is doing is not just to escort the ships out, but it's to prevent any Iranian oil or any other export products from coming out. That's very important for the economic pressure in Iran that'll either change their regime, or it'll change their regime's policies.

So, this is a conflict. Make no mistake about that. But a nuclear armed Iran is an existential threat, not just for the region but for the world economy.

I'm very proud of President Trump, not just kicking this can down the road like previous presidents have done, but saying we've got to end that capability. We've got to reset the Middle East so it can have generations of peace and prosperity.

RADDATZ: Well, let's talk about gas prices. Right now, the average is $4.10 a gallon. A year ago, the Labor Day average was $3.16 a gallon. Diesel prices are also soaring.

Just a few weeks ago -- you mentioned President Trump -- he dismissed the increase in gas prices as just a tiny bit.

Let's play this for you.

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: For you to pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline, just remember, you're doing it so that a very evil country cannot have -- a country really it’s the number one state sponsor of terror in the world. We don't want to have them have a nuclear weapon. So, remember that when you have to pay a little bit more, you're at $4, it’s OK. I mean it's -- I'm not -- I'm not -- I'll never apologize. I did the right thing.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

RADDATZ: OK, it's been more than six months of paying higher prices. And there is also no sign of a nuclear agreement. You talk about that. President Trump talks about that. But where's the sign that they're going to have a nuclear agreement?

WRIGHT: There may not be a nuclear agreement. It may be simply destroying their capabilities to do it. An agreement may await the next administration in Iran. We simply don't know that.

But I think what the president was communicating there is how critically important this is. If Iran has nuclear weapons, the Middle East, the world is a wildly different place than it is today. And the Trump administration, as you heard last year at Labor Day, incredibly low gas prices at the end of peak driving season.

Yes, they're higher today, but we're doing everything we can to push them down. We changed refinery -- refinery specs recently so that American refineries can produce more gasoline and diesel.

New York, Connecticut, California, and other Democratic-run states decided not to adopt those. Their goal is to raise energy prices. California's had that goal for quite some time.

RADDATZ: Mr. Secretary, I've got to stop you there. You said we may not get a nuclear agreement. So how do we keep them from having a nuclear weapon? Just keep bombing when they build things up?

WRIGHT: You have to destroy their capabilities to do it. They built a massive missile infrastructure to manufacture missiles, which you see them firing today, but they don't have the capability to build more missiles. We are degrading their capacity to develop nuclear weapons and ultimately to deliver them if they develop them.

It’s -- it is 47-year-long effort. This is not trivial, but the United States will get the job done and we will work in cooperation with our allies in the region. And I think you'll see countries from around the world joining this effort as well.

RADDATZ: And realistically, let's again talk about gas prices. How soon should Americans see these go down? We know you have this deal with Venezuela that could take years before we see any effect of that.

Will we see a change before the midterm? When will we see those gas prices go down?

WRIGHT: Well, if you look at the futures prices, you wanted to buy today in bulk gasoline for two months out in November, it's about 35 cents cheaper than it is today. So the marketplace thinks gasoline prices are going to move meaningfully lower. So trust the market, certainly don't trust my predictions.

But we're doing everything we can to grow the production of gasoline as we pass Labor Day tomorrow, you start to see demand decline as we move out of summer driving season. So the Trump administration is leaning in heavily in that area.

And Venezuela, I wouldn't discount it. Things there are going well ahead of plan. Venezuelan oil exports are up 50 percent. Their total national production is up 25 percent and billions of dollars of new investment has been announced.

The Trump administration is working on all fronts from the Gulf of America to Alaska to onshore in the U.S., to our allies in the hemisphere, to grow energy production, and long term to reset energy prices lower and more stable supply chain.

RADDATZ: And, Mr. Secretary, just finally, you negotiated this Venezuelan deal with Delcy Rodriguez, who was vice president under the Maduro regime, the regime that the Trump administration attacked as a socialist dictatorship. Why do you trust her?

WRIGHT: Well, I wasn't the negotiator on the deal, but she -- we have a lot of leverage over Venezuela. We control the sale of oil outside of their country.

So right now, they are forced to work in partnership with us, and they are working in partnership with us. It's drawing billions of dollars in investment and it's transforming that region from a region of conflict to a region of commerce. I think the momentum going that direction, whoever is ruling Venezuela, is quite strong, very, very positive for the hemis -- for the Western Hemisphere.

RADDATZ: Thanks very much for joining us this morning, Mr. Secretary.

WRIGHT: Thank you, Martha.

RADDATZ: And as the Iran war drags on, this week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has faced mounting questions about his leadership. His army secretary resigned Monday. And that’s just the latest in a series of resignations and firings in Hegseth’s tumultuous tenure at the Pentagon.

(BEGIN VIDEOTAPE)

RADDATZ (voice-over): For Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, it was a week of unwelcome headlines and renewed calls for his ouster.

Republican Thom Tillis posting on X, “I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country. I urge the president to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent, rather than diminish it.”

That followed the resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll after repeated disagreements with Hegseth over the firing of multiple senior military officers, including the highly respected Army chief of staff, Randy George, and a slew of others.

REP. DON BACON, (R) NEBRASKA: He has not been a very good leader in many -- in many ways.

REP. MIKE LAWLER, (R) NEW YORK: It is critical, frankly, that Pete Hegseth come forth and talk about exactly why these changes have been made.

RADDATZ (voice over): Before resigning, Driscoll warned President Trump about the impact of Hegseth firing senior military leaders and blocking promotions as well, according to sources familiar with the matter.

VICE ADM. NANCY LACORE, FORMER CHIEF OF U.S. NAVY RESERVE (RET.) & (D) SOUTH CAROLINA CONGRESSIONAL CANDIDATE: One year into that position, I was removed by Pete Hegseth. I was not given a reason.

RADDATZ (voice over): One Navy vice admiral Hegseth fired, Nancy Lacore.

LACORE: There was no notice other than, you know, being called down to a senior Navy four-star’s office on Friday afternoon and given the message. And that was it. An hour later, I was out of the Pentagon.

RADDATZ (voice over): Lacore, now running as a Democrat for the congressional seat currently held by Representative Nancy Mace.

LACORE: The abrupt end to my service really just wasn’t sitting well with me. And I, you know, service has been my entire life. And I just wanted to continue serving. Running for Congress was another way of serving our country.

RADDATZ (voice over): And it is not just those who have been ousted from the Pentagon who have concerns. “The Washington Post” reported that top military leaders have advised Hegseth that prolonging large scale operations against Iran was unsustainable and risked weakening our ability to confront threats elsewhere and at home. Leaks have infuriated Hegseth, but they keep coming, reportedly prompting him to polygraph Pentagon staff.

“The New York Times” reporting late Friday that some 50 members of the U.S. military’s joint staff have been polygraphed because of leaks about critical munitions shortages. Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell telling ABC News, the department “does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters but takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly.” Hegseth has repeatedly claimed the U.S. has won the war and depleted Iran’s missiles, while denying the U.S. has a problem.

LAIR: That is my hope, and that they will remember 9/11 as something that happened not to a nation, but to regular people just like them.

CRANFORD: It shows that like even during a terrorist attack, real humans, firefighters, even people on the ground, still wanted to help the people that were in a -- literally, a burning building.

O'BRIEN: In our darkest hour.

CRANFORD: In our darkest hour, people still wanted to help.

O'BRIEN (voice-over): A day that young people like Micayla didn't live, but one that forever shaped their future.

O'BRIEN: What do you think people your age should take away about that day?

CRANFORD: Ask your parents about that day. Ask how it made them feel and get a deeper knowledge of it. Because it's a day that will truly live on in history that will forever be talked about.

(END VIDEOTAPE)

RADDATZ: And it will indeed. Our thanks to Jay. And be sure to tune in to full coverage on ABC News this Friday, September 11th, throughout the day as "25 Years Later, America Remembers."

And at 8 p.m. Eastern Friday, a special "Tribute in Light" live from Lower Manhattan in partnership with the 9/11 Memorial & Museum.

We'll be right back.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

RADDATZ: That's all for today. Thanks for sharing part of your Sunday with us. Check out "World News Tonight" and have a great Labor Day.

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed could win rural Michigan if GOP doesn't show up | Opinion
news.text:
SHIAWASSEE COUNTY ― Amid a sea of farm-plated pickup trucks, the annual Shiawassee County Fair brought together folks in American flag T-shirts, screeching chickens ‒ and Abdul El-Sayed buttons.

Take a look at the electoral history of Shiawassee County and you can easily see that, overall, it’s red. President Donald Trump defeated Kamala Harris here 61% to 38%. But state legislative races are a bit more colorful; the latest district maps puts some of Shiawassee County’s farm country in a district with the city of East Lansing.

And that makes Shiawassee County an interesting place to think about the politics of affordability ‒ and how people here are feeling about the November election.

MORE BITELY: Michigan voters shouldn't treat a con-con as a protest vote

While walking through the fair’s exhibit barn, I noticed booths for the Shiawassee County Republican Party as well as the Shiawassee Democrats. And in a world where the people who show up win, the Democrats had the GOP beat.

On five separate occasions, I walked through the barn, each time looking to see whether the booths were staffed, if buttons and stickers were being handed out or ‒ the all-important metric ‒ whether candy was disappearing from the tables.

Each time, the Democrats' booth had at least two people, talking to fairgoers and handing out materials. The Republicans' booth remained empty.

In politics, the people who show up usually matter

Now, sitting at a booth at a county fair doesn’t necessarily indicate much of anything. But it gives a clue as to how motivated people are to get the message out.

I talked with Karen Grennell, a school board trustee from Perry who had done a number of shifts in the Democrats' booth.

“Almost all the people I’ve talked to here have had the same concern: affordability, cost. Families are struggling right now. They are living paycheck to paycheck and still can’t make ends meet,” Karen told me from behind the well-stocked swag table in the fair booth. “This election coming up in November is so important, I fight for the working class and I will to my last dying breath, and families ‒ all the families ‒ are hurting.”

I have to admit, I can see it.

Inflation and cost of living increases have hit everyone, but the cost of actually growing food has increased as well.

Why is beef more expensive? Why does it cost $5 for five slices of bacon? Because nearly everything that goes into producing it and getting it to your grocery store has gotten more expensive.

And the person that most people blame is President Donald Trump.

Everything costs more, and voters know it

It makes sense. As president, Trump gets credit for the good and is blamed for the bad. Unfortunately for him, the bad is currently outweighing the good in very obvious categories.

A gallon of regular gas is topping $4.10. Diesel, which powers the trucks moving goods from place to place, costs even more. And the push by the environmental movement toward electric vehicles doesn’t necessarily solve the affordability problem when Michigan’s utility prices are among the highest in the nation.

In rural Michigan, those costs compound. Caring for animals and harvesting crops requires fuel, equipment and electricity. And simply getting from home to work, school or the grocery store can mean driving 30 minutes or more, and a gallon of gas, in each direction.

The fertilizer bill is political, too

Then there are the costs farmers have even less control over.

Take potash, a key fertilizer for Michigan crops like sugar beets. When we fight with Canada and impose tariffs, the cost of that fertilizer can rise. According to The Fertilizer Institute, a trade association representing fertilizer manufacturers and related industries, 85% of U.S. potash imports come from Canada.

BITELY: The toughest question for Benson and Brinks is Lansing

The major alternative source outside Canada? Russia, another country with which our relationship is hardly friendly. And the ongoing war with Iran also continues to play a role in keeping fertilizer prices high.

All of this adds up to a pretty simple political argument: Rural Michigan is expensive, and decisions made by our government in Washington can make it more expensive.

The affordability argument is Democrats' to win

After my trip to the fair, I reached out to the Shiawassee County Republicans. Dan McMaster, the GOP County Chair, responded in his personal capacity.

“For some candidates, the excitement level is extremely high, like Mike Rogers, our former state senator and congressman. Two years ago it was hard to get people to take his yard signs. Last week, it was the biggest, or most, in demand,” he wrote to me by email. “I speak for myself on this, and not as chair, but I believe Republicans are looking forward to the fight this fall, to go head-to-head against the extreme liberal and progressive Democrat candidates on the ticket. (Jocelyn) Benson, (Winnie) Brinks, (Will) Lawrence, (Stephen) Schlaak and Emily Olsen, who is running for road commission, and when on city council she wouldn't rise for the pledge or invocation.

“We needed something to motivate turnout of low-propensity evangelicals and the Dems have given it to us,” McMaster wrote. “In Shiawassee County, Sharia Law and the celebration of 9/11 doesn't go over well.”

For the record, none of the Democrats running do either.

If I were a Democrat running for office, I’d redouble my efforts in places like Shiawassee County. I’d talk less about trying to turn a red county blue and more about something voters there experience every single day: what it costs to fill the truck, fertilize the field, feed the animals and put dinner on the table.

And I’d make Republicans explain why those costs keep going up. If they don’t, El-Sayed buttons might not look quite so out of place at the county fair.

Free Press contributing columnist Andrea Bitely is the founder and principal of Bitely Communications, a Lansing-based public affairs firm specializing in political, corporate and crisis communications. From September 2025 through May 2026, she served as director of communications for former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan's now-ended independent gubernatorial campaign.

news.title: Midterm Countdown: Republicans find their boogeymen
news.text:
Democrats are counting on voter disaffection over high gas prices and President Donald Trump’s sinking poll numbers to help them flip the House and possibly the Senate.

But they’ve also been plagued by far-left activists who are distracting their affordability message.

Plus, ongoing redistricting battles in Missouri and a legal tussle over Trump’s mail-in voting executive order are still in flux as voters in North Carolina begin receiving absentee ballots. 

Republicans find their boogeymen

For years, Republicans had a recurring star in their TV ads and campaign messaging: Nancy Pelosi. The former Democratic speaker was the longtime villain, a mainstay in ads as Republicans linked Democratic candidates to her to paint them as radical and out of touch. 

She was so toxic, in some areas, that many battleground candidates specifically campaigned on the promise they would not vote for Pelosi as speaker. In 2019, as Pelosi’s unpopularity roared, 15 Democrats refused to vote for her on the House floor. Many of them had just been elected in battleground districts — such as Abigail Spanberger, Mikie Sherrill, and Elissa Slotkin, all of whom would later seek higher office. 

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) is not unpopular enough — or well known enough — to be the next boogeyman. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) have appeared in some ads over the last few cycles.

But neither are as inflammatory as Hasan Piker, the socialist Twitch streamer who has become a staple in Republican midterm messaging over the past month. Piker, who has been criticized for his vehemently anti-Israel posture, is an outspoken supporter of Abdul el Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s Senate race. 

Piker’s past controversial comments, including saying that “America deserved 9/11,” have given Republicans ammunition with which to damage Democrats. He’s also become a central part of their contrast message. 

Vice President JD Vance took aim at el Sayed and Piker during a recent campaign swing through Michigan. 

“My message to Abdul el Sayed is: You can pal around with terrorist sympathizers, and you can say that America deserved 9/11, or you could empathize, not with the children who were targeted at Temple Israel, but with the attacker,” he said. “These are all despicable things, but they’re all things that the people of Michigan will judge you on based on your record.” 

A Republican strategist also said they anticipate making regional villains so that their messages resonate. 

In New York, for example, socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani figures to take a lead role in negative advertising. 

The National Republican Campaign Committee said Democrats “own every radical position” taken by the polarizing figures.

“Vulnerable House Democrats have tied themselves to the most unhinged socialists in their party, from Zohran Mamdani to Hasan Piker,” NRCC Spokesman Mike Marinella told the Washington Examiner in a statement. “Now they own every radical position, every insane statement, and every socialist policy that comes with them, and we’re going to hang that record around their necks like an anvil all the way to Election Day.”

Missouri madness notches Democrats a surprise win 

Democrats scored an unexpected win the first week of September after Missouri’s state Supreme Court unanimously blocked the GOP’s new congressional map. 

The ruling requires Missouri to use its previous map for the November elections, effectively restoring Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s (D-MO) Kansas City-based 5th Congressional District. 

At the center of the case was an effort by opponents of the new map to put it before voters through Missouri’s referendum process. Under the state constitution, voters can petition to approve or reject laws passed by the legislature. Opponents gathered enough signatures to force a referendum on the new congressional map, which meant the map could not take effect unless and until voters approved it.

But Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins rejected the referendum, arguing that congressional redistricting legislation was not subject to the state’s referendum process. The Missouri Supreme Court — dominated by Republican appointees — ruled the secretary of state erred in making the decision.

As a result, the court put the new map on hold until voters can approve it in November. Even if it passes, the new map will not take effect until 2028.

Republicans already hold six out of the eight districts in Missouri. The new map was set to give the party a seventh district. 

The ruling creates an unusual situation for November. Missouri held its August congressional primaries using the new districts, but voters will cast their general election ballots under the old lines.

Missouri Republicans said they will appeal the decision to the Supreme Court, though the case centers heavily on the Missouri Supreme Court’s interpretation of the state constitution.

Trump sends Cabinet officials across the country

Trump is leaning on members of his Cabinet to help carry his message beyond Washington as Republicans enter the final stretch before the midterm elections.

The travel is part of a broader effort to energize voters and defend Republicans’ narrow congressional majorities amid concerns about the economy and the Iran war. Sending administration officials into key states also gives GOP candidates prominent surrogates who can promote specific pieces of Trump’s agenda to local voters.

War Secretary Pete Hegseth has become one of the administration’s most active political messengers. He campaigned for Kentucky Republican Ed Gallrein, who defeated Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY), and appeared at the Iowa State Fair for a veteran-focused fundraiser with Rep. Zach Nunn (R-IA), Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-IA), and GOP Senate candidate Ashley Hinson. Nunn and Miller-Meeks are fighting to keep their House seats, while Hinson is running in a competitive race for an open Senate seat.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was in Michigan on Monday alongside Vance and Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson for a MAGA Inc. event. Also in attendance were Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers and other GOP candidates for Congress and statewide office.

The travel has not always allowed Cabinet officials to stick to the administration’s preferred message. Energy Secretary Chris Wright visited New Hampshire last week to promote the administration’s push for additional natural gas pipelines but faced questions about gasoline prices that have climbed to roughly $4 a gallon.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins ran into another politically sensitive issue during a swing through Iowa. While seeking to shore up support among farmers, Rollins was forced to address Trump’s move to allow foreign beef imports, a decision that has drawn criticism from cattle ranchers.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. traveled to Tampa with Sen. Ashley Moody (R-FL) to roll out a new school nutrition initiative. Kennedy remains a valuable messenger to the “Make America Healthy Again” voters who helped expand Trump’s coalition, even as some activists have grown frustrated with administration decisions, including its approach to glyphosate.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meanwhile, is headed to North Carolina to speak before the Charlotte Economics Club. Bessent has become a go-to administration voice on economic policy at a time when Republicans are looking to reassure voters about the economy while also confronting criticism surrounding the costs of the Iran war.

One notable administration figure has been largely absent from the political circuit. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, widely viewed as a possible 2028 presidential contender, has mostly stayed away from campaign events even as many of his Cabinet colleagues have taken increasingly visible roles in the midterm push.

The barnstorming also gives Republicans an opportunity to put other faces on Trump’s agenda at a moment when the president’s own standing with voters could weigh on the party in November. Some administration officials may be better positioned to reach constituencies where Trump has lost ground, allowing Republicans to campaign on his policies without making every midterm contest a referendum on the president himself.

Red state Democrats are good on Kamala Harris

Democrats running key red state races have a clear message for former Vice President Kamala Harris: stay away.

A growing number of Democrats have preemptively rejected an endorsement from Harris this cycle.

Campaign spokespersons for Rob Sand, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee in Iowa, and Iowa Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek told the Washington Examiner they don’t want an endorsement from Harris or for her to appear on the campaign trail with them. 

Throughout Trump’s three presidential campaigns, Iowa has tracked Republican after it voted for former President Barack Obama in 2008. 

But Democrats see an opening to flip the governor’s mansion and retiring Sen. Joni Ernst’s (R-IA) seat blue as the GOP struggles to counter their affordability message. 

The Cook Political Report ranked the Iowa gubernatorial race and the Senate race as toss-ups.

Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola also rejected a Harris fundraising email sent on her behalf. “Mary isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 — her focus is and always will be Alaska,” a Peltola spokesperson told a local news outlet.

Harris dismissed the rejections as part of the election race in an interview with MS Now. 

“We need to win,” Harris said. “I have run locally, I’ve run for statewide office and obviously nationally, and these candidates know what they need to do to win, and I would expect nothing less.” 

But not all Democrats are shunning Harris. 

San Diego City Councilmember Marni von Wilpert is running for California’s 48th Congressional District. She said that Harris will come to her district. 

Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford is expected to host Harris for a canvass lunch in Las Vegas as he seeks the governor’s mansion. 

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) also hosted the former vice president for a private “Women for Ossoff” call. And Harris recently endorsed Rep. Chris Pappas (D-NH) in his Senate race in New Hampshire. 

Harris remains a 2028 Democratic front-runner according to most polls, meaning Democrats won’t be able to continue to shun her if she launches a third presidential bid. 

The next big campaign issue

August saw data centers emerge — and then explode — as a campaign issue. Anti-data center sentiment nearly propelled socialist state Rep. Francesca Hong to victory in the Wisconsin gubernatorial Democratic primary, but a stunning consolidation effort around David Crowley, who is pro-data center, helped the moderate Democrat over the finish line in early August. 

President Donald Trump has championed data center construction but has sent candidates mixed messages on how to talk about them. 

He told reporters before a campaign stop in South Carolina last month that he was fine if Republicans disagreed with him on data centers. The president has said he supports building them and they bring “tremendous income” for communities. 

‘If a Republican is against the data center, that’s OK with me,” said Trump, offering a softer stance if Republicans disagree with him. 

He then took an aggressive position on social media earlier this week, writing that the “only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.”

“If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” he wrote. “The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.”

The issue has become a concern for Republicans. The National Republican Senatorial Committee in August released a memo arguing that voters are sour on data centers and that they risk becoming a liability for Republicans in competitive races, particularly Sen. Jon Husted’s (R-OH) reelection campaign. 

“More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck. If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one,” the memo wrote of Husted’s race. 

The memo said the “companies that need these projects built” must fix this problem, effectively asking the corporations to invest in changing voter sentiment. 

So far, Republicans have had a mixed response, with candidates adopting platforms best reflecting the sentiment of their communities, but the issue is almost certain to dominate between now and the November election. 

What the prediction markets say

Prediction markets are increasingly viewed as a real-time gauge of political sentiment. Unlike traditional polling, they aggregate real-money bets on political outcomes, often capturing shifts in sentiment quicker than surveys.

At this stage in the 2026 cycle, Kalshi gives Democrats an 85% chance of retaking the House, while Republicans have a 53% chance of keeping control of the Senate.

Meanwhile, Polymarket is slightly more bullish on Democrats, giving the party an 89% chance of retaking the House and a 52% chance of winning the Senate.

The GOP is in final preparations for the Republican Midterm Convention […]

news.title: Hunter Biden: ‘I may have to’ run for president in 2028
news.text:
Former President Biden’s son, Hunter Biden, said that he may have to consider a 2028 presidential run amid speculation on who the Democratic nominee could be.

On an episode of "The Cats Roundtable" released Sunday, radio host John Catsimatidis asked Biden if he had any plans to run for president, to which Biden answered, "If I get your endorsement, I may have to." 

When asked the same question earlier, the former president's son replied, “I haven’t made up my mind.”

“The truth of the matter is that I think we have an incredible bench,” Biden said, mentioning Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) before declaring: "I love Gavin Newsom, personally.”

Newsom, California's Democratic governor, has been open about his interest in seeking the top office. In October, Newsom told CBS News's Robert Costa that he would be “lying” if he said he wasn’t considering a bid for the White House after the 2026 midterms.

Other potential contenders include Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), former Vice President Kamala Harris, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

Biden expressed during the interview that no matter who the candidate is, he wants “the next president to commit to one thing: to commit to adhering to the rule of law. To commit to the idea that we believe in this constitutional republic and the aspirations of normal Americans.”

“I truly, truly want whoever is our president to succeed. But particularly succeed in keeping this country safe. That’s their primary responsibility,” he said.

An August survey from Emerson College and The Hill ranked potential match-ups between possible GOP and Democratic presidential candidates and found Biden's pick in a decent position.

Newsom held small leads over both potential Republican nominees — Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio — unlike Ocasio-Cortez, who trailed both candidates. 

Biden added that what he cared about right now “is the 50 million Americans that are still suffering, sick … with their addictions.”

While acknowledging his struggles with substance abuse issues, the former president's son noted in the interview that he recently celebrated seven and a half years of sobriety.

news.title: Can Democrats flip Florida in 2026?
news.text:
Last month, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon won the state’s Democratic Senate nomination in a major upset over her better-funded opponent, retired Army Lt. Col. Alex Vindman. Her victory was quickly slotted into a narrative about the Democratic Party’s insurgent progressive movement, which has triumphed in House and Senate primaries in Michigan, Colorado, New York, and elsewhere. 
But while Nixon supports progressive policies, she argues there’s more to the story than a simple progressive-versus-centrist tale. She says that she out-worked and out-organized her opponent — and that Floridians across the political spectrum are hungry for change. 
Vox’s Astead Herndon invited Nixon on a special pop-up episode of America, Actually to break down how she won the nomination, why she thinks there’s a path to victory in what many analysts believe is a solidly red state, and what she wants to get done as a senator if she prevails in November.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
[Media: https://open.spotify.com/show/0xv3qPaQ9tu0l5zyz7AQkx?si=2d127db4ff3644af]
Why do you think your victory took so many by surprise?
It took so many by surprise because people both tend to underestimate a Black woman — especially a progressive Black woman in politics — and then one who wasn’t able to raise as much money. But as a former single mom for 12 years, I know how to make a dollar stretch.
This win is attributed to good old-fashioned grassroots organizing. I am a former union organizer. I am a community organizer, and I know the importance of people power and talking to people and getting them energized about why they should vote and why they should see themselves in this country.
How much would you ascribe your win to the type of politics that you’re describing here versus the progressive policies that you championed? Should we take this as a sign that Medicare-for-all and “abolish ICE” have strong support in Florida?
It’s all of it, right? It is the hard work that we put into this race to raise awareness about who I am and the policies and positions that I stand for, which are policies and positions that the majority of hardworking, everyday people stand for. 
Just because we want access to quality healthcare and affordable housing and fully funded public schools, they try to fear-monger and make it seem as though we are communist and we’re not.
We are not communist. We are people who want to put hardworking, everyday people in power so that they can determine and shape what our communities look like and what our economies look like. There’s nothing radical or extreme about that.
Democrats are still dismissing your chances to win a general election. Prominent pundits have said that Democrats should not invest in Florida, and that would amount to wasted money. Political forecasters moved the race in the Republican direction after your primary victory, arguing that the progressive politics makes it easier for Republicans to win in a state like Florida.
I wanted to ask about electability. Can you give me the case for how you can win a statewide race amongst such skepticism? 
The same way that I was able to win a primary being outspent and out-raised 18 to 1. I am building a very unique, diverse coalition of people. We’ve had Republicans and independents that crossed over in the primary to vote for me in the primary. They also volunteer in our campaign. They’ve made donations. 
We literally have a bunch of Republicans and libertarians who have been stating that they are voting for me because they like that I am no-nonsense. They appreciate that I am trying to put a check on what is coming out of Washington, DC, all of the cruelty and the corruption, and that is the winning message.
Look, we’re up against a woman, [incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody], who allowed the theft of $10 million. She allowed money to be stolen from medically needy and low-income kids, to be diverted toward two citizen-led ballot initiatives that actually caused us to not have better health in our communities. 
People are frustrated, and that’s all Ashley Moody has done — just look out for herself, her campaign donors and these billionaires. People are ready for elected officials to stop bailing out these big businesses [and] actually look out for everyday people.
In November 2023, you introduced a resolution to the Florida House calling for “the immediate de-escalation and ceasefire…in Israel and occupied Palestine.” It was rejected 104 to 2. And it earned you some bad blood with some of the members of the Florida Jewish Caucus. The chair actually said that the resolution was born out of ignorance and antisemitism.
Obviously, the Democratic Party base has shifted on that issue over the last several years. There’s been an open discussion about whether Joe Biden and Kamala Harris did themselves damage in the 2024 election by not breaking more explicitly with Israel’s actions in Gaza.
Do you think that was a mistake for Democrats?
I would say yes. I would say that we have to have really uncomfortable conversations amongst our different communities and we just have to talk. But I feel that they did do a disservice in regards to just going along with the AIPAC lobby.
You had mentioned that you don’t support sending any money or any weapons to Israel at this moment, but I also wanted to ask about things like BDS, the movement to boycott, divest, or sanction Israel. Is that something you support?
It is. I’m a Black woman who is a descendant of slaves, and who is the descendant of people from the civil rights movement, and I know how we used boycotts and we used protest to gain our civil rights for our community. So I’m fully supportive of that.
You repeatedly said that you don’t support defunding the police on your website. It says that you support demilitarizing the police. And that “real safety comes from good jobs, strong schools, affordable housing, and healthcare for all — not from more cameras, more cages, and more agents.”
What is the difference between that and defunding?
Whatever folks think the difference is. I’m not going to box myself in because I understand how they’ll try to cut and clip things with me saying certain words.
But doesn’t that sound a little bit like lessening the resources that go to police to focus on other things? I mean, that sounds a little like the same thing.
It sounds like I know that is my position. I want to defund Flock cameras because bad cops are stalking their ex-girlfriends and ex-boyfriends. And so to-may-toe, to-mah-toe. I literally said this before and that is what I am for. I’m not trying to get clipped in any kind of way.
Let me ask you this way. I appreciate the focus on root causes, and I think you’ve laid that out that that’s where you want the energy to go — that real public safety comes from focusing on the things that cause people to commit crimes in the first place, but those often take a long time to show effect.
If we’re talking about the root causes of crime, what is the message to someone whose community is unsafe right now that does not include policing?
What I would say is, making sure that we invest in making sure people have more jobs and we invest in community control of the police. I totally believe in civil review boards and that type of thing, but I believe in making sure that people’s most basic needs are met. 
One of the things that I believe could help that right off the bat is things like universal healthcare, or at a minimum, extending the ACA subsidies so that we can drive down these healthcare premium costs. Or fully funding these programs that allow people to have access to first-time homebuyer programs. 
I was a single mom for 12 years, and I took part in the first-time homebuyer program that was funded from the federal government. That trickled down to the state and then to the local government. That helped me with down payment assistance as well as closing costs and those types of programs. We need to put policies in place that are allowing people to be good.
We need to push for universal child care. For every $1 that is invested by the government, it puts $3 back into the economy so parents can get to work. They can be able to make sure that they have money to put their children in different programs. We need to invest in programs to keep our children off the streets.
There’s been so much effort to put you in one of the boxes that have defined the Democratic ideological battles — DSA versus establishment. I hear in this interview how that doesn’t neatly fit with what it seems like you’ve done in Florida. 
Where do you think this campaign fits into the ongoing question of where do Democrats go next?
We’re coalition builders, we’re aggregators. Folks should know, I was a vice chair of a local Democratic Party. I was also the field director and the political director with the state party. I have never fit in a box. I was a union member and I also led a statewide organization that was straight-up progressive.
We need all these things to fight back against this Donald Trump regime. Look, this man is not going to leave willingly in 2028. He’s created a paramilitary force in the form of ICE that is getting away with shooting people and slaughtering them on camera while they’re masked without any accountability. They’re pushing to see how far they can go.
Granted, Black people have been getting slaughtered on camera without accountability for a while, but now they are doing it to people who aren’t just Black, who aren’t just Latino. They are banking on us being normalized with what’s happening.
First lady Michelle Obama says, “They go low, we go high.” I’m saying, “We get loud, we push back. We organize stronger and harder so that we can win and change this country and build a new vision for the next 250 years, where we have a Florida and an America for all.”

news.title: A Political Operative on the Verge of Self-Deportation
news.text:
In an age of YouTube ads and paid political-content creators, the notion might seem quaint. But González, who’s thirty-one, has made it her job to figure out how to use the mail to help elect Democrats. On a projected slide deck, she flipped through examples of mailers that she and her firm had worked on: there was the familiar ALEXANDRIA ¡OCASIO! CORTEZ logo, a lotería-themed postcard that read “VOTE FOR OUR COMMUNITY, VOTE FOR RUBEN GALLEGO,” and another one, paid for by the Dolores Huerta Foundation and decorated with Día de los Muertos imagery, that read “VOTA PALOOZA.” González knows the rules of the game, and shared some loopholes that she’s learned along the way—for instance, that political-action committees cannot coördinate with campaigns, but that campaigns can post information, in hard-to-find corners of their websites, about what kind of advertising they happen to need help with. After González concluded her talk, an attendee asked about something she had mentioned earlier—that she was Salvadoran, and living in the U.S. under Temporary Protected Status. “I’m so sorry to hear that,” the person said. González, seeming impassive, said, “It’ll work out how it needs to.”
González is one of an estimated two hundred thousand Salvadorans whose legal immigration status is set to expire on September 9th, and one of about a million immigrants in the widening gyre of the Trump Administration’s delegalization drive. For González, who has lived in the U.S. nearly her entire life, the date is a brick wall of a deadline. “That’s when I sell my house, I sell my car, I buy a ticket, I pack everything I own, I get rid of everything I can’t take with me,” she told me.
Unlike most immigrants in America, González has a job that puts her in rooms with powerful people. As a partner at the consulting firm Solidarity Strategies, she tries to help Democrats win some of the most consequential races in the country, including James Talarico’s campaign for Senate, but also smaller names in red districts trying to flip the House. Her biggest client this cycle is the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which has paid her firm more than a hundred and eighty thousand dollars this year, according to the Federal Election Commission. She’s grown friendly with Tony Cárdenas, a client and former congressman from California, who officiated the wedding of her mentor and boss, the political consultant Chuck Rocha. After the seminar, González returned a missed call from Cárdenas, who’d inquired about a New Yorker reporter asking to speak to him. “If you’d be willing to talk to him, there’s nothing I’m really avoiding,” she told Cárdenas in a voice mail. She turned to me: “He probably doesn’t want to say the wrong thing.”
González is introverted, but comes across as warm and cheerful. She smiles while she talks, except when she’s on the verge of tears. Her colleagues at Solidarity Strategies think that she’s good with people, so they’ve put her in charge of dealing with candidates, Party officials, and campaign committees. “Chuck Rocha don’t need to be over there if I’m gonna have a candidate screaming at me and telling me that I’m stupid,” Rocha, the firm’s founder, who appears often, as a straight-talking, cowboy-hatted commentator, on CNN, told me. “That does not go good for Chuck. But Daysi has a way to tell them that they’re stupid, and to do it in such a nice way.”
Temporary Protected Status gave González the ability to work, but did not qualify her for federal financial aid when applying to college. The Church helped in that regard: González chose Brigham Young University-Idaho, which is heavily subsidized for Mormons. She was there in the lead-up to the 2016 election, and she recalls a professor noticing her Spanish name. “You better hope Trump doesn’t win,” she remembers the professor saying derisively. When González sought legal advice, a lawyer looked her “dead in the eyes” and asked if she had a boyfriend who she could marry for a green card. But she didn’t want her future to depend on one person; she knew of people whose spouses used the threat of deportation to manipulate them. She’d been dating someone for about a month at the time, and broke up with him soon after.
In 2019, González was introduced to Rocha, who had a reputation as a cultivator of Black and brown political talent. Rocha, who is Mexican American, saw something special in González’s immigrant background. “These types of people have had to figure out how to make it through life any way—they could figure out how to make a piece of mail,” he told me. He hired González to help with social media, manage clients, and do administrative work, but, in time, she started designing ads herself. Soon after she joined, the firm was hired to help run Bernie Sanders’s 2020 Presidential campaign, which meant that González was the only person handling the rest of the clients at the firm’s K Street office; she became an equity partner within a few years.
After that election, as she built her life in a capital governed by Democrats, González grew alienated from her church. “It was jarring to be living here, going through the immigration struggles that I’m going through, and then, like, high-ranking leaders in the Church are MAGA. Why am I associating myself with this?” And she began to worry about her status again in 2024, as the second Trump Presidency came into view. After Kamala Harris became the Democratic nominee for President, the polling looked bleak enough that González sat Rocha down to talk, anxious that she’d have to leave the country.
The life that González had made in America over twenty-five years—the college degree and the career, the house in northern Virginia she owns with her sister, the Honda HR-V she paid off last year—was possible because the question of her status had settled into a cycle of unstable predictability. New Presidents continued to find that conditions in El Salvador merited the extension of the “temporary” status, and she dutifully paid the fees and filled out the paperwork every eighteen months and pay steep fees. (By itself, T.P.S. doesn’t provide a path to a green card or citizenship.) Trump attempted to cancel the status during his first term, but the courts had ruled it unlawful; after he won again, Joe Biden, during his last week in office, approved another eighteen-month reprieve. González had never got this close to zero before. This past Monday, less than two weeks before the extension was set to expire, she packed up some belongings she’d kept at her office: three pairs of high heels, a pair of fuzzy slippers, a tube of toothpaste. “Having to take some stuff out of my desk—like, I never got that far, other times.”
Rocha said that he would, but he didn’t; he just stopped telling her about it. As recently as last month, he said, he had talked privately with people who worked in Trump’s White House. “Send me her stuff,” one staffer said, “but also know that this can cut both ways if I raise this too high.” Rocha has many friends in Washington, but his attempts to change González’s situation have left him feeling powerless. “You mean I can’t call a senator? I can’t call the chairman of the Hispanic Caucus and just fix this shit?” he said, raising his arms incredulously. “No matter how many important people you know, no matter how much money you think you have, that you’ve made at this little firm—none of that matters.” He grew agitated thinking of Obama’s decision not to pursue immigration reform when he had legislative majorities. “Now me and my team are paying for that,” he said, before quickly adding, “nothing against Barack Obama.”
Rocha wishes that the elected officials his firm has worked for would give speeches from the House floor to emphasize that the people ensnared by Trump’s policies are not criminals. But Democrats have become more tentative to speak on immigration since the Obama years. Andrea Flores, who worked in the Obama Administration and served as a border official under Biden, told me that Biden lacked interest in pushing legislation to regularize the status of longtime residents. The House Minority Leader, Hakeem Jeffries, she pointed out, didn’t even mention immigration in a recent press conference announcing an agenda of Democratic priorities should they retake the majority. “There may not be an immediate electoral gain in prioritizing immigration,” Flores said, “but there is an absolute electoral risk and loss by allowing the system to be as dysfunctional as it is, and allowing the Republican Party to continue to weaponize that dysfunction against Democrats.”
Rafael Collazo, the executive director at UnidosUS Action Fund, a Latino civil-rights advocacy group and a client of González’s, told me that her case should underscore a “failure of leadership” in D.C. that “we’re all responsible for.” “But,” he added, “in particular, Congress, and, in particular, the people that claim to be more progressive on immigration issues—the Democratic Party, Democrats in Congress—they haven’t done enough. None of them have done enough.”
González is planning to go back to El Salvador—a place where she has few relatives left, and where, although Rocha has offered to keep her as a remote worker, she’s not sure she’ll be able to keep her job. Then she’ll try to immigrate to another country, such as Spain. (Spain offers a digital-nomad visa, with a fast-tracked path to citizenship for Latin American nationals—“Like a sort of reparations program,” she said.) She’d started documenting her final month of T.P.S. on Instagram, initially hoping to catch the attention of someone in government, but she now thinks of the videos as more like “diaries.” In one, she notices that she’s out of rice, and laughingly considers whether she should bother buying another bag.
On work calls, González told me, there’s now a preamble: “ ‘I’m so sorry you’re going through this, like, let me know if you need anything. But when is that mail going to drop? Have you had the chance to get the invoice out?” And even though she works to elect Democrats, González said that the candidates whom she helps elect may have little to say about her case. “I don’t know what more they could add, other than like, ‘Damn, that sucks,” she said, before putting on a politician voice: “And that’s why I want to win and fight for immigrants.” Cárdenas, when reached by phone, said something along those lines: “Should Democrats do more? Yes, and the opportunity to do more is really going to be in their hands when they control the House, when they control the Senate, when they control the Presidency.” While in Congress, Cárdenas helped González navigate her immigration status and the attendant anguish that came with it. He left after twelve years in 2025, feeling like he could’ve done more—but, then again, he added, “I worked my butt off, man . . . and you only have so much staff.”
How would you spend your last days in America? For González, the natural answer involves BTS concerts. She’s become a superfan since Trump was reëlected, and has found community in the fandom. On Friday, she boarded an early flight to Los Angeles to attend the final show in the North American leg of the K-pop group’s world tour. She had gone to the band’s concert in Baltimore about a month earlier, and got home at four in the morning. “As the concert was ending, people around me were probably, like, ‘Oh, she’s crying because the show’s over, she’s a diehard fan,’ ” she recounted. That was part of it, but also, “I knew that I was going back to this mess, and that the countdown’s started, right?” Her favorite BTS song is “00:00 (Zero O’Clock),” a melancholy anthem about uncertainty, and starting over. ♦
news.summary: Daysi González, who works to elect Democrats, is gearing up to leave the U.S. as soon as this month. She wants her own party to pay attention.

news.title: RNC Comes to Texas as Trump Stronghold Under Threat
news.text: President Donald Trump's Republican National Convention is coming to Texas this week as the GOP confronts an uncomfortable reality: The longtime conservative stronghold is emerging as one of the biggest battlegrounds of the 2026 midterm elections. The GOP is holding the unprecedented midterm Republican convention in Dallas on September 9 and 10. The convention is part of an effort to motivate the party's base and thwart midterm losses, as polls show many Americans have soured on the Trump administration amid growing frustration with inflation, the economy and the war in Iran. Trump's declining national approval rating has fueled Democrats' hopes that 2026 could be the year they flip Texas as polls show tightening statewide races. Democrats have long dreamed of flipping Texas, the largest Republican-leaning state, but have consistently come up short. While Republican margins narrowed throughout the 2010s, the state again moved rightward in 2024, giving Trump a 14-point victory over then-Vice President Kamala Harris. But that hasn't stopped Democrats from making Texas a top target in the November midterms. The Lone Star State's Senate race has become one of the most competitive and expensive of the midterms as Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton finds himself in an increasingly close race against Democratic state Representative James Talarico. Paxton unseated Senator John Cornyn in the primary. The race has become a pure toss-up, according to the Cook Political Report, as a flurry of recent polls give Talarico a lead. Republican Governor Greg Abbott also finds himself facing a more competitive race than expected against Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa, though polls and forecasters still favor the incumbent to win reelection. Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas Republican strategist, told Newsweek he believes Republicans have reason to worry about the Lone Star State. "This year, there are signs that the Democrats are very competitive," he said. Newsweek has contacted the Paxton and Talarico campaigns for comment via email. Republicans Raise Alarms in Texas Steinhauser said there are two major reasons Democrats may be able to make Texas competitive this year—affordability and the data center revolt happening in Texas and across the country. The rising prices of energy and groceries are having a real "impact on people," he said. "Given what's going on in the world with the economy, with the war in Iran, and then with the sort of data center backlash happening, I think that this is definitely a competitive year for Democrats," Steinhauser said. Other Republicans have also expressed concerns about Texas in the midterms. Senator Ted Cruz has said the election is a "real fight." "We could lose Texas. This is a five-alarm fire right now, and every Republican, every conservative, every non-nuts commonsense Texan needs to understand the crazies are coming out in force," he said during an interview last month on the Lt. Dan podcast, hosted by Texas Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick. Sid Miller, the state's outgoing agriculture commissioner, told The Washington Post that data centers could become an issue for the GOP. "I've been leading the charge against these data centers for a year or more, and it's all falling on deaf ears. It's going to hurt us in the midterms. I think we could lose some statewide races," he told the newspaper. Abbott, however, has downplayed concerns about Democrats flipping Texas in the midterms. "There's a choice at the ballot box. And when those voters go in, they're going to choose between common sense that's offered by Republicans versus the crazy that's offered by the Democrats," he told ABC News in August. Mark Jones, a politics professor at Rice University in Houston, told Newsweek that the Senate race is "very competitive." He said that while the governor's race is "more competitive than our recent gubernatorial races," Abbott still has a lead. "A common denominator for all of these races, for all races in Texas, and this also applies nationally, is the unpopularity of Donald Trump in terms of disapproval of his handling of his job as president, handling of the economy, and handling of a wide range of policy issues combined with his high unfavorables," he said. Texas Democratic Party chairman Kendall Scudder told Newsweek that Democrats are "building a movement focused on lowering costs, protecting health care, and delivering real results for working class Texans." "While Republicans come to Dallas to celebrate Donald Trump and double-down on their bluster, Texas Democrats are organizing around what actually matters to people in this state," Scudder said. Democrats Set Sights on Senate Race The Senate race between Paxton and Talarico has become particularly concerning for Republicans. Texas has not elected a Democratic senator since 1988, but Democrats believe Talarico could break the GOP's winning streak. The Cook Political Report last month reclassified the race as a pure toss-up, as polls showed a close race and Paxton faced financial challenges. Paxton, with the support of Trump, unseated Cornyn in the primary after arguing that the four-term senator was insufficiently MAGA for such a conservative state. Cornyn's office told Newsweek on Thursday that he would not be attending the convention. Despite the president's endorsement, some Republicans have long worried about Paxton's electability. The attorney general has faced a series of personal scandals, including his 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House over articles alleging bribery and abuse of public trust. The investigation stemmed from a proposed whistleblower lawsuit settlement, involving several of Paxton's former aides who said they were fired after accusing the attorney general of accepting bribes and other misconduct. Paxton has denied any wrongdoing. Paxton was acquitted in the Texas Senate. He has described the impeachment as a "weaponization of our political system" that was "designed to intimidate, bankrupt, silence, and punish me for representing the voters instead of the entrenched political establishment." The state attorney general has also recently faced scrutiny over a Waco plea deal that prosecutors in his office offered a man accused of repeatedly sexually abusing a young boy. Those scandals have "really eroded public support" for Paxton, even among Republican voters, Jones said. "At the end of the day, it will be those Republican voters who will determine whether Paxton or Talarico wins," the politics professor added. Republicans, on the other hand, have tried to portray Talarico as being out of step with voters in the state, pointing to his past remarks about God being nonbinary and his supposed meatless diet to cast him as out of touch with Texans. Talarico responded to claims that he is vegan by saying, "I've been eating barbecue since before Ken Paxton's first indictment." According to Steinhauser, though Cornyn has performed well in the past, there might not be a significant difference if he had won the nomination. "I think in this particular case, the environment is very tough, and I think that Cornyn would probably be right where Abbott is, which is a little better maybe than Ken, but I don't think there would be a huge gap," he said. What Do Polls Show? Paxton Faces Funding Gap Finances have emerged as a key issue for Paxton in the Senate race, as he trails Talarico in fundraising. It's a critical issue in Texas, a large state that includes several expensive media markets in cities such as Dallas and Houston. Candidates failing to raise significant funds could struggle to get their message out to voters. This fundraising gap could have major national implications. Texas is going to be one of the handful of seats that determine whether Democrats or Republicans hold a Senate majority after the midterms. Democrats face a daunting map this year, so if they manage to flip Texas, their path to a majority will become easier. Talarico's campaign said he raised about $30 million in the second quarter of 2026, while Paxton's campaign said he raised about $9 million, according to the Texas Tribune. Republicans have acknowledged the issue and signaled that they would like Trump to spend money to boost Paxton. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, said on Fox News that he is "hoping the White House will become engaged," noting Texas is a must-win for Republicans if they want to keep the Senate. "Because Texas is such an expensive state, we're going to need the president and his team to be engaged there and to be putting resources into that race," he said. Jones noted that the National GOP has so far not intervened to save Paxton. He said: "Senate Republicans have actually intimated at least that their super PAC will not be spending heavily in Texas and support Ken Paxton, that this is a situation that Donald Trump gave them Ken Paxton, and therefore if someone's going to save Ken Paxton, it's going to be Trump's super PAC." He warned that Paxton would need "considerable assistance" from national political action committees to win in November. In a Federal Election Commission filing on Saturday, MAGA Inc. revealed in an independent expenditure report that it has spent $10 million in the Texas Senate race. Abbott Favored in Governor Race In the gubernatorial race, Abbott is still viewed as a favorite over Hinojosa and has led polling, but the race looks closer compared to other recent election cycles. Texas has no term limit for its governor, and Abbott has held the office since 2015. While he's not particularly liked by Democrats in the state, he is not seen as a particularly controversial governor for Republicans and is well-positioned to retain support among traditional GOP voters. Steinhauser said Abbott is likely to overperform Paxton "by a bit." Jones noted that Abbott is likely to spend nearly $100 million by the time the campaign is over, and that Hinojosa "doesn't have anywhere near the amount" of funding that Abbott has. Hinojosa told Newsweek that Texans "are tired of almost 12 years under Greg Abbott." "As governor, I will secure the American Dream by saving public schools and putting money back in your pocket. Greg Abbott is at the weakest he has ever been," she said in a statement. "Even lifelong conservatives are 'breaking rank' after seeing Greg Abbott turn his back on their communities with his voucher scheme and his data center takeover. Texans are ready for change." Data Centers Become Key Issue The governor has been focused on data center development, an issue that has become central to voter concerns. Abbott last month said he had paused approvals for new proposed data centers while regulators conduct a comprehensive audit. On ABC News' This Week, he said the facilities had "dug their own grave" and had not done enough to engage in communities. It's also an issue that gives him some independence from Trump, who has been vocal in his support of data center development. Just this week, the president said communities that reject the projects risk becoming "backwards and poor." Eduardo Leal, Abbott's campaign press secretary, told Newsweek that some of the governor's top priorities are affordability and protecting Texans' "safety and quality of life." Leal said the governor has directed regulators to ensure data centers do not take water needed by communities or power needed by the grid, do not disrupt neighborhoods and rural communities, and pay for their own electricity infrastructure. "Any project that fails to meet these standards will be denied connection to the Texas grid. He has also called for eliminating data center sales tax breaks. Simply put, data centers must pay their own way, and Texans must come first. Governor Abbott will work with the Texas Legislature to codify these commonsense standards into law," he said. Hinojosa has also been critical of data centers and has urged Abbott to call an emergency legislative session to pass protections for Texans. During a CBS News interview, she described the pause as an attempt by Abbott "to protect his reelection chances," saying he had "invited hundreds of data centers into Texas with the largest tax break in the whole country." "Texans have real concerns. These hyperscale data centers have hyperscale impacts on our communities when it comes to our grid, our water and just our way of life," she said. "Texans want protections and rightfully so." What Do Polls Show? GOP Hopes Convention Will Boost Candidates Texas state Representative and former Texas House Speaker Dade Phelan told Newsweek that conventions are usually about energizing the base and getting out the vote. He said he’s concerned about signs that Democrats appear more enthusiastic than Republicans, pointing to Democrats outperforming Republicans during the Texas primaries and polls showing that they are “more energized” to vote. “This is a fundraiser, it appears to me, and a very expensive one at that,” he said. “I'm curious of how it's going to actually get out the vote, and that's what matters is energizing your base.” He said the headwinds are “much, much stronger” this year compared to 2018, the last so-called “blue wave,” and that he doesn’t know how interest in the convention may translate into votes in November. The convention could have a "marginal positive impact," Steinhauser said. "It will energize the base," the Republican strategist continued. "It will help them financially." However, he said the event is unlikely to have a lasting impact among swing voters and independents. The impact also depends on what Republicans say from the stage. Steinhauser said the GOP must come across as appealing to swing voters, not just the base, to be successful. Jones described the convention as a "double-edged sword." "Since Republicans are inextricably linked to Donald Trump, it probably does help having him here if for no other reason than to mobilize people who voted for him back in 2024," he said. How Conservative Is Texas? Texas has long held a reputation as being one of the most reliably Republican states in the country, but things have been shifting in the Lone Star State. From 2000 to 2020, Republican margins shifted from 21 points to fewer than 6 points at the presidential level. The state shifted back rightward in 2024, backing Trump by 14 points, but Democrats are still hopeful about the prospects of "Blue Texas." Population booms in cities such as Austin, Dallas and Houston, as well as their suburbs shifting leftward in the Trump era have helped make the state less overwhelmingly conservative and would be key to helping the state flip this year. But Texas also has a large concentration of Hispanic and Latino voters that shifted significantly toward Trump last year. In 2020, Latino voters backed Joe Biden by 17 points over Trump; however, in 2024, they backed Trump by 10 points, according to CNN exit polling data. Latino voters are now a critical swing group, and whether Democrats can win back those voters could determine their fate in November. If Talarico wins this year, it could give Democrats more reason to invest in the state in the future, Jones said. It could make it easier for Democrats to recruit quality statewide candidates and raise money from national Democrats to further make the state competitive in future cycles, he added. What Happens Next Republicans are set to gather in Dallas on September 9 and 10 for the convention, where Trump and other GOP leaders are expected to make the case for keeping Texas firmly in Republican hands. With polling showing competitive Senate and gubernatorial races, both parties will be watching closely for signs of whether the event helps energize voters ahead of the November 3 elections. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Shakeema Edwards.
news.summary: Trump’s Texas convention arrives as GOP fears grow, with Paxton slipping and Democrats sensing a rare chance to flip the state.
